# THREE
## TRACTS.

**I. REMARKS** upon this **QUESTION:** Whether the appearances in the Old Testament were appearances of the true **GOD** Himself, or only of some other spiritual being, representing the true **GOD** and acting in His name.

**II. AN ESSAY** on the **Divine Presence.** <note>original: "Schechinah"; a Hebrew term referring to the "dwelling" or "settling" of God’s presence among His people.</note> Or, considerations on the divine appearances mentioned in the Scriptures.

**III. TEXTS** of **SCRIPTURE** relating to the **Word**, <note>original: "Logos"; a Greek term used in the New Testament to describe the divine nature and pre-existence of Jesus Christ.</note> considered.

---

->*By the late Reverend and Learned*<-
### MOSES LOWMAN.

---

->LONDON:<-
->Printed for J. NOON, at the *White Hart*, near *Mercers' Chapel*, in *Cheapside*.<-
->1756.<-
-><insert>1756</insert><-

### The PREFACE.

He considered this to be of greater importance and necessity because he was fully convinced that there were constant allusions in the writings of the New Testament to the rituals, facts, sentiments, and forms of expression found in the Old Testament. He believed that, because of this, significant light could be shed upon some of the principal doctrines of Christianity.

This will appear fully evident from the following papers, in which the learned author endeavors to explain many passages relating to the person and glory of Christ. He does this by considering and describing the nature and circumstances of the *Shekhinah* <note>original: *Schechinah*; a Hebrew term referring to the visible manifestation of the "settling" or "dwelling" of the divine presence of God</note>, or the glorious appearance of the Great God in the most ancient times of the world. # REMARKS
### ON THE
## QUESTION, etc.

<image-desc>An ornamental square drop cap 'T' containing a crest or shield depicting two birds and a building, surrounded by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

The nature of the divine appearances, as they are described and represented in several passages of the Old Testament, is in itself a subject of high importance; the consideration of which may serve to shed light on many passages of the New Testament which relate to some principal doctrines of *Christianity*. It has been the occasion of a question of equally great consequence: whether the true God did not himself appear in, and with the visible symbols of light, and the audible voice of the oracle, which are usually called the *Shekinah* <note>original: "Schechinah"; a Hebrew term referring to the "dwelling" or "settling" of the divine presence of God, often manifested as a cloud or pillar of fire</note>; or, whether this *Shekinah* was not some inferior spiritual agent, or intel-

<header>REMARKS on</header>

-ligent being, who, in those perceptible symbols, personified the true God; who appeared, spoke, and acted as His angel or messenger, and so acted in His name alone. And therefore, [the question is] whether the person appearing in the *Shekinah* <note>original: "Schechinah"</note> was a separate spirit, or, as some suppose, the pre-existent soul of the Messiah?

To make way for a clearer answer to this question, it may be helpful first to explain it as each side seems to understand it.

Those who believe these appearances to have been the proper and real appearances of the true God do not mean that God did or could become visible in His own nature; since He is spiritual, He is for that reason absolutely invisible. Nor do they suppose that an infinite spirit could actually move from one place to another, or leave one place for another where He was not already. They only mean that God, on some particular occasions, manifested Himself to others through specific actions, which He intended to be taken as the marks and evidence of a special and particular presence.

<margin>*George Bull, Defense of the Nicene Faith, Section 4, chapter 3, section 5.*</margin>
This is a sense of a divine presence that seems easy to understand, and we find it described this way by *Bishop Bull*: "Therefore God, who spoke to Moses out of the burning bush, did not appear in any way other than was fitting for God; that is, not by passing from place to place, or in such a way that He was confined within the narrow limits of some location, but [by a] visible appearance..." <note>original: "Deus igitur, qui Mosen e rubo ardenti allocutus est, non aliter apparuit, quam Deum decuit; hoc est, non de loco in locum transeundo, aut ita ut loci alicujus angustiis clauderetur, sed Speciem vi-"</note>

> ... his hands, and said: "O Jehovah, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in the heavens or on the earth."

It is clear that Solomon intended his prayer to be directed to the one true God—to that infinite Being whose presence is universal—even though, in a meaningful sense, he was also uniquely present in his Temple. It is to this divine presence that Solomon directly addresses his prayer.

<margin>Verses 18, 19, 20, 21.</margin>
> "But will God really <note>original: "in very deed"</note> dwell with men on earth? The opinion of the <term>Church Fathers: Influential early Christian theologians whose writings established foundational doctrines.</term> on this subject is very different from the way this question has recently been explained and defended. The interpretation being argued for now is actually a new and modern opinion, no matter how much it claims the support and sponsorship of the venerable Church Fathers. Indeed, even if the judgment of the Fathers had been completely clear and obvious on this point, that alone would not be a conclusive reason. For as a noble author justly observes:

*Essay on*
*Dispensations,*
*Addition,*
*p. 133.*

> "The opinion of the Fathers would not be of great consequence if the Scriptures did not seem to plainly agree with us in all of this."

It is therefore further suggested and affirmed that there are three considerations from the Scriptures themselves that clearly show it was not God himself, but only some inferior spirit or angel representing God, who appeared to Moses and the <term>Ancestors: Specifically the Old Testament patriarchs such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</term>. They are these:

**First:** God is represented as always invisible—one *whom no person has seen, or can see*.

**Second:** The appearance is described as the *Angel of the Lord* and is expressly titled as such, which seems inconsistent with an actual appearance of God himself.

**Third:** Several of these appearances are attributed in Scripture to Christ, who speaks and acts in his Father's name.

But what then, we might be inclined to say, is meant by these expressions, *that no man has seen God at any time, or can see Him?* It would seem that something more is meant than what is common to all spiritual beings, such as angels and the souls of men. The Hebrew scholars <note>original: "Doctors"</note> then did not understand "seeing" God as the sight of any physical <note>original: "bodily"</note> form. They did not believe that because God is invisible, He could not reveal <note>original: "manifest"</note> Himself through sensory symbols of His presence. Nor did they think that because God was invisible—whom no living man could see—there must have been some visible spirit representing Him in the appearance of the *Shekinah* <note>original: "Schechinah"; the term refers to the dwelling or settling of the divine presence of God</note>. It seems clear that they had no such notion at all. On the contrary, whoever carefully examines their concept of the *Shekinah* will find that they did not perceive it to be some other spirit representing God, but the true God revealing Himself through material symbols of light and fire. This is how the previously mentioned *Maimonides* explains their views:

the Scriptures, are called *Angels of the Lord*, *who do His will*. The contrary supposition—namely, that they are the same and not different spirits—proves that they are one and the same God. For just as the application of the divine appearances can only prove a representation on the supposition that the Word <note>original: "the Word"; the Logos, or pre-incarnate Christ.</note> was not God when he appeared as God, so the contrary supposition will serve equally well to prove that since He *was* God, there was no room for any "representation" at all.

Indeed, the true reason why the Scriptures apply the divine appearances of the Old Testament to Christ seems to be a very different thing and is, I believe, to be accounted for in a very different manner.

Order should be observed in outward actions, just as it is observed in the principles from which they proceed.

We have an example of this in the natural order of our own powers as spiritual beings. We possess the powers of understanding or intelligence, of reason or wisdom, and of will or action. We recognize a corresponding <note>original: "answerable"</note> order in how these are used. We say with great appropriateness <note>original: "Propriety"</note> that some are acts of the understanding, some are acts of wisdom and counsel, and some are acts of the will and active power.

In the same way, when we consider the infinite Mind as Father, Word, and Spirit, we can also conceive of a distinct order in their actions; and according to this order and <term>economy</term> <note>the way God manages his relationship with the world</note>, we can attribute those actions to each specifically. This, I believe, will show the appropriateness of such expressions just as effectively as the theory that some different intelligent being appeared to impersonate the true God as his angel or messenger. I think this explanation is actually necessary, because the same Scriptures describe those appearances and actions as the appearances of the *true God*, even while ascribing them to the *Word*.

# THE QUESTION

The Presence of God therefore in this place must be God himself <note>original: "αὐτος ο Θεός"</note>—as the Septuagint <note>The Seventy; the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> justly translate it; and that in direct opposition to an *angel* acting in His name and place.

Before I leave this observation, it may be useful just to take notice of one thing more: that *Mimra* <note>An Aramaic word meaning "The Word," often used in the Targums to describe God's personal action or presence.</note>, a word so often used in the *Chaldee Paraphrases* <note>Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible, also known as Targums.</note>, does in that language most properly signify "himself" <note>original: "αὐτος, Ipse"</note>. *The Word of the Lord* <note>original: "Mimra de Adonai"</note> properly therefore signifies God himself. *The Word of Jehovah* <note>original: "Mimra Jehovah"</note> is used as a demonstrative particle, showing that *Jehovah* is spoken of in His proper person. This is an accepted sense of the expression, even when another sense is also argued for. Of this there are innumerable instances. I shall only mention one:

<margin>Genesis 9:17.</margin>
> *And God said to Noah, "This is the token of the covenant which I have established between Me and all flesh that is upon the earth."*

Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> expresses it this way:
> “This is the sign of the covenant, which I have established between my *Word* <note>original: "Mimra"</note> and all flesh.”

On the whole, it would seem that the ancient interpreters, who were best acquainted with the *Hebrew* expression and the doctrines of the *Jewish* Church, understood the appearances of *Jehovah* to be appearances of God himself, not of some other being in His name and as His representative. <header>the QUESTION.</header>

*Solomon’s* prayer <margin>Numbers 10:35, 36.</margin> was exactly consistent with the ancient form. When the Ark, the seat of the Divine Presence, moved forward, *Moses* said: "*Rise up, Jehovah, and let your enemies be scattered; and let those who hate you flee before you.*" And when it rested, he said: "*Return, O Jehovah, unto the many thousands of Israel.*"

There is not a single form of expression in any of the most solemn parts of worship that is not directly offered to the Person dwelling in the Temple as the object of it. There is not the slightest hint that these acts of worship were not properly offered to Him, or that they were designed for another person whom He only represented. He is always addressed as *Jehovah*, always praised as *Jehovah*, and all the worship of the entire Church is addressed to him—not only as a proper object of worship, but as the only proper object of it. 

If we suppose He was only a representative, who would be able to give a plausible reason why the entire worship of the Church should be directed immediately to Him? Why would He be addressed under the names *Jehovah*, *Lord of Hosts*, and *the most high God*, without any mention of any other or higher object of worship? Who can explain, or allow for, the appropriateness of the words of *Daniel* under such a theory when he prays: "*O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, listen and act; do not delay for your own name's sake, for your city and people are called by your name*"? <note>Daniel 9:19</note> This would be impossible if none of these titles properly belonged to the Person being addressed...

# REMARKS on

Fourth, if these were the appearances of an angel, or a spirit representing the Most High, and there was no declaration of such a representative, it would be contrary to the chief and principal design of the whole *Mosaic* Institution <note>original: "Mosaical Institution"; the system of religious laws and practices established through Moses</note> of religion. One main view and fundamental principle of that dispensation was to draw the *Jews* away from worshiping—or addressing their solemn worship to—the one true God by means of inferior beings, or through their hands. One intention of that Law was to serve as a guard against the then-prevailing idolatry of their neighboring nations, which consisted of worshiping God through demons <note>original: "Dæmons"; in this context, referring to lesser deities or spirits thought to act as intermediaries</note>, or by the mediation of angels and separate spirits who were supposed to be appointed by God as the guardians of mortal men. The Law of *Moses*, therefore, directed the worship of the *Jewish* Church in all its parts to the true God himself, and taught the people to acknowledge the Most High alone as the proper object of worship.

It was the first and fundamental article of the faith of that Church that there is only one true God. And it was the first Commandment that *they should have no other gods before him, or beside him.* They were to worship Him, and Him only. Therefore, it seems plain—on the assumption <note>original: "Supposition"</note> that the being present in the *Shekinah* <note>original: "Schechinah"; a Hebrew term referring to the visible manifestation of God’s presence or "dwelling"</note> was only an angel, or some inferior spiritual being representing the Most High—that an imme-

But we are also to remark that the Scriptures mention particular messages on extraordinary occasions, delivered sometimes by angels and sometimes by prophets. Because these messages show more than ordinary notice of people and things, they are understood to denote a unique presence of God on such occasions, and are expressed accordingly in the Holy Scriptures. For instance, *Moses* and *Aaron* were sent with a direct message from God to *Pharaoh* to inform him that God had taken particular notice of the afflictions of *Israel*, and had sent a specific or extraordinary command to him to release them. *“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let my people go”* (Exodus 5:1).

And in this same way, he was also sent to the children of *Israel* with this commission: *“Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: I AM has sent me to you”* (Exodus 3:14). When *Moses* had carried out <note>original: "executed"</note> this commission, the people expressed the understanding they had of it in this manner: *“And the people believed; and when they heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel, and that he had looked upon their affliction, then they bowed their heads and worshipped”* (Exodus 4:31).

"Angel" is properly a name of an office, not of the nature or essence of any being. "It should be known," says Ambrose, <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note> "that 'Angel' is a name of office, not of nature. You ask the name of this nature? It is spirit. You ask the name of the office? It is angel. From what it is, it is spirit; from what it does, it is an angel." <note>original Latin: "Sciendum est, ait Ambrosius, quod Angelus est Nomen Officii, non Naturae. Quaeris hujus Naturae Nomen? Spiritus est. Quaeris Officii? Angelus. Ex Eo quod est, est Spiritus; ex Eo quod agit, Angelus."</note>

The common sense of the word *Angel*, however, is to denote an order of spiritual beings of great understanding and power, superior to the souls or spirits of men. These are the same as the "separate intelligences" <note>A philosophical term, derived from Aristotle and used by medieval scholars, to describe non-physical minds that exist independently of matter.</note> of the philosophers; or those whom *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> describes <margin>Philo, *On Dreams*, p. 455 or 586. *On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain*, p. 102.</margin> as "...most pure and excellent souls, who have achieved greater and more divine thoughts—these are what other philosophers call demons, <note>In ancient Greek, "daimones" referred to divine spirits or lesser deities, not necessarily evil beings.</note> but the sacred word <note>Referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> usually calls angels." <note>original Greek: "ψυχαὶ καθαρώταται καὶ ἄρισται, μειζόνων φρονημάτων καὶ θειοτέρων ἐπιλαχέσαι — ταύτας δαίμονας μὲν οἱ ἄλλοι Φιλόσοφοι, ὁ δὲ ἱερὸς λόγος ἀγγέλους εἴωθε καλεῖν."</note>

That there is an innumerable company of this high order of spiritual beings, ancient pagan theology supposes and the Scriptures very plainly declare. He further explains the observation in the *Genesis Rabbah* <term>Bereshith Rabba</term> <note>A classic collection of ancient Jewish interpretations and homilies on the Book of Genesis.</note>: "God does nothing unless he has first consulted about it in, or with, the 'family above'" <note>original Latin: *Familia superiori*; referring to the heavenly host or divine council</note>. Or, as it is further observed: "Wherever it says in Scripture, *And the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: ויהוה (*V'Adonai*)</note>, it is understood to mean 'He and His court of justice'" <note>original Latin: *Domus Judicii*</note>. 

The meaning and intent of all these sayings is not as if God actually spoke, thought, or sought the advice and consideration of others, or was aided by anyone’s opinion; for how could the Creator be helped by his own creature? Rather, they declare to us that even the smallest parts of the beings of this world—down to the creation of the limbs of animals, exactly as they are—happen through the mediation of angels; because all natural powers and faculties are 'angels.' How truly ruinous and harmful is ignorance of this matter! 

In this way, he also explains another tradition in the *Genesis Rabbah*: "The tradition is that one angel never performs two missions <note>original Latin: *Legationes*</note>, nor do two angels ever perform a single mission."

Thus this most learned of the Jewish Masters, and the most skillful in their language and customs, explains the meaning of the word *Angel*. He shows at the same time how useful this knowledge is for a right understanding of many expressions used by Jewish writers, and of many of their maxims formed upon them.

Our critical interpreters often make use of these maxims and expressions to explain or illustrate the language of Scripture. But for want of attending to this specific sense, they have sometimes applied to separate spirits <note>Distinct spiritual entities or supernatural beings</note> what was only meant to describe particular natural or animal powers, the actions of irrational beings, or even the effects of fire and wind.

So, if the language of the *Jewish* masters <note>original: "Jewish Masters"; referring to prominent Jewish scholars and rabbis</note> is useful for explaining the language of Scripture on this subject, I believe we can be reasonably satisfied that this was their understanding of the word *Angel*. According to their judgment, we should apply it in this sense to certain passages of Scripture. To be sure, it is far from being a new or insignificant opinion, as it is found in the writings of the greatest antiquity and authority. Many of their famous maxims are founded upon it and can only be understood correctly through this lens. This is also the doctrine of the *Samaritan* school. <note>The Samaritan school refers to the religious and scholarly traditions of the Samaritans, who follow their own version of the Torah.</note>

However useful the explanations of the *Jewish* masters may be for clarifying the language of Scripture in some cases, they should only be viewed as other similar aids of criticism <term>criticism</term> <note>In this context, "criticism" refers to the scholarly study and interpretation of historical texts.</note>. They may go far to clear up and confirm a meaning that is already probable and supported by other factors, but they can never impose a meaning on Scripture that contradicts clearer and more compelling evidence. It may be appropriate, then, in this inquiry (setting aside *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204) was a highly influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> and the *Jewish* writers for the moment) to see what we can find from the phrasing and expression of the Scriptures themselves, using the standard methods for interpreting ancient authors and languages.

These expressions cannot, I think, be easily interpreted as the actual action of an independent spirit <note>original: "separate Spirit"</note> using a sword in any natural way. Therefore, if we turn to a prophetic, symbolic <note>original: "emblematical"</note> style—as I believe is appropriate and even necessary when interpreting how visions are expressed—it represents this plain truth to *David*: that God had punished *Israel* for his sin with a severe and deadly pestilence, as he had threatened, but that he remembered his people with mercy and would not punish them as much as they deserved. 

In this way, I believe the appearance of the angel is best explained: not that he literally killed the people with his sword (which would mean the punishment was the physical act of an independent spirit), but that this vision assured *David* that this severe plague was a deliberate punishment for his sin, and that God had sent it among the people in an extraordinary way.

Similarly, when an angel is sent to protect *Daniel*, what interpretation seems most natural and appropriate? Is it that the ferocity of the lions was restrained by a special act of divine power, or that it was the physical act of an independent spirit to shut the lions' mouths and muzzle them so that they might not hurt the prophet?

If it is still argued that a common opinion exists—that God does not usually act directly himself, but instead acts through the immediate agency of angels as his ministers—it must be admitted that the Jews have such a maxim: *For you will not find that God has done any work, except by the hands of some angel* <note>original Latin: "Non enim invenies Deum ullum opus fecisse, nisi per manus alicujus Angeli."</note>. Yet the true meaning of that maxim, as we have already seen from *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher whose work *The Guide for the Perplexed* deeply influenced rationalist interpretations of the Bible.</note>, is to establish the specific sense of the word "angel" that I have been trying to explain: namely, that it refers to everything God appoints and uses to fulfill his will. This includes the powers and effects of inanimate and irrational things, as well as other beings. To insist in all cases on the common definition of the word "angel"—as an independent spirit <note>original: "separate Spirit"</note> performing its own specific action—is to misunderstand the meaning of the Hebrew masters, as well as the language of Scripture. In fact, that maxim is so far from supporting the literal view of independent spirits that it is actually based on an opinion directly opposite to it.

## CHAPTER I.

### *The general concept of the most prominent manner of God's special presence, or the* <term>Shekhinah</term>.

HAVING previously established this much concerning the meaning of the word *Angel*—the reason for which will become clear as we proceed in this inquiry—let us endeavor to determine, as clearly as we can, how the Scriptures represent the most prominent manner of God's special presence, or the *Shekhinah* <note>The term *Shekhinah* is derived from the Hebrew root for "dwelling" and refers to the divine presence or manifestation of God, often associated with a cloud of glory.</note>.

Although this subject has often been touched upon by men of learning, and some things relating to it have been explained here and there in passing, I believe it has not been examined as carefully or explained as fully as it deserves. This study is of great use in providing a true understanding of the nature, privileges, and worship of the Jewish Church. It also helps to explain many things in the Christian state that are taught to us in words and expressions alluding to this concept of the *Shekhinah*, and which are indeed taken originally from it. The word "to dwell" <note>original Greek: σκηνου (*skēnou*), meaning to pitch a tent or dwell.</note>, so often used in the New Testament and in some important doctrines of Christianity, is the same in meaning, and almost in sound, as the word "to dwell" <note>original Hebrew: *Schacan* (shakan).</note> from which *Shekhinah* is derived,

God promises in Exodus 29:45: *And I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will be their God.* <note>original Hebrew: ושכנתי בתוך בני ישראל (*Veshecanti betok Beni Israel*)</note>. And the Arabic version says with the same intention: "And I will cause my light to dwell among the children of Israel." <note>original Latin translation of the Arabic: *Et habitare faciam lucem meam inter Filios Israel*</note>.

How consistent with these forms of expression are the words of St. John, when he heard a great voice from heaven, saying: <margin>Revelation 21:3.</margin> *Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people. And God himself shall be with them, and be their God.* "Behold, the tabernacle of God..." <note>original Greek: ἰδου η σκηνὴ του Θεου (*idou hē skēnē tou Theou*)</note>.

As this carries the notion much farther than Maimonides <note>A 12th-century Jewish philosopher and physician.</note>, it is also an explanation, as I understand it, that is contrary to his view. By his "created light" <note>original Latin: *Lux creata*</note>, Maimonides seems to mean a light produced for the particular purpose of that specific manifestation, rather than the first light ever made, set aside as if it were only fit for such use upon any occasion whatsoever.

Upon this general account of the *Shekinah* <note>The divine presence or "dwelling" of God.</note>, most people have formed an idea of it as an extraordinary appearance of God, in, by, or with an extraordinary appearance of light.

<margin>Thomas Burnet, *On the State of the Dead* <note>original Latin: *De Statu Mortuorum*</note>, page 304.</margin>
A learned author has expressed it this way: "The *Shekinah*, taken in a broad sense, is used to designate any notable effect of the divine presence. Less broadly, it denotes the divine presence under some specific form or visible sign. Finally, in the strictest sense, it denotes the majestic presence, as they say, displayed in some luminous, fiery, or glowing matter." <note>original Latin: *Schechinah, late sumpta, usurpatur ad designandum quodlibet effectum notabile Præsentiæ divinæ: Minus late, præsentiam divinam, sub aliqua Specie, aut Signo visibili, denotat. Denique strictissime, Præsentiam Majestaticam, ut aiunt, in materia aliqua lucida, ignea, aut candescenti, exhibitam.*</note>

From this *Shekinah*, which in the strictest sense denotes the presence of God's glory and majesty, the Temple is called the place where His honor or glory dwells. *Psalm 26:8*. "The place of the dwelling of your glory" <note>original Hebrew: מקום משכן כבודך (*Mekom Mishcon Chebodcha*); original Greek from the Septuagint: τοπον σκηνωματος δοξης σε (*topon skēnomatos doxēs sou*).</note>.

It is also called the face or presence of God, *Psalm 68:8*. "The face of God" <note>original Hebrew: פני אלהים (*Penei Elohim*); original Greek from the Septuagint: απο προσωπε τε Θεε ισραηλ (*apo prosōpou tou Theou Israēl*), meaning "from the face of the God of Israel."</note>. Thus, when God promises His *Shekinah* to Israel in *Exodus 33:14*, it is called His "Presence."

### the SCHECHINAH.

*And He, the Lord, said, Panai* <note>Hebrew for "my presence" or "my face."</note>, *my Presence shall go with you.* The *Seventy* <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> had good reason, considering the intent and meaning of the passage, to translate this as, "I myself will go before you" <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸς προπορεύσομαι*</note>. However, *Onkelos*, the *Chaldee* <note>Aramaic</note> *translator*, uses the term *Shechinthi* <note>Aramaic for "my dwelling" or "my presence"</note>, meaning "my *Shekinah*" or "my Majesty." For this reason, the *Arabic* version seems to have translated it as, "My light shall go with you" <note>original Latin: *Lux mea ambulabit*</note>.

And this is how we should understand the expression in verse 11: *And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face.* This seems to be an explanation of verse 9: *And it happened, as Moses entered the Tabernacle, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the door of the Tabernacle, and the Lord talked with Moses.*

To mention one more thing regarding the general concept of the *Shekinah*, we may observe that because of this presence, the *Tabernacle* (and later the *Temple*) was the place the Lord chose out of all the *Tribes* to put His Name there. Deuteronomy 12:5 says: *But you shall seek the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put His Name there—His very dwelling place—and there you shall go.* Based on this promise, *Solomon* prayed at the dedication of his Temple (1 Kings 8:29): *That Your eyes may be open toward this house night and day, even toward the place of which You have said, "My Name shall be there."* And God Himself later expressed the sanctification of the Temple in this way—

# CHAPTER II

## *The various specific representations of the* Shekinah, *up until the full establishment of* Temple worship *under* Solomon.

Following this general account of the Shekinah <note>original: Schechinah; the divine presence or "dwelling" of God</note>—the most glorious appearance of God’s majesty and special presence—let us move on to a more detailed consideration of the main passages of Scripture where it is described more specifically. By examining the suitability of the language and the way these manifestations of God’s presence are presented to us, we will build a foundation—based on actual facts—for a proper understanding of these appearances. 

This is a better foundation, I believe, than uncertain guesses based on long-standing prejudices <note>In this context, "prejudices" refers to preconceived notions or traditional biases in interpretation</note>. These prejudices have become so old that they are now seen as too respectable to ignore, even though they originally stemmed from a misunderstanding of proper biblical criticism regarding the style and language of Scripture, or from a lack of care in comparing the various scriptural passages related to this subject. I believe both of these factors have significantly contributed to the obscurity <note>meaning: confusion or lack of clarity</note> of this topic.

## CHAPTER II.

### *The Various Specific Representations of the Shekinah, until the Full Establishment of Temple Worship under Solomon.*

Following this general account of the Shekinah <note>original: Schechinah; the divine presence or "dwelling" of God</note>, or the most glorious appearance of God’s majesty and special presence, let us move to a more detailed examination of the main passages of Scripture where it is specifically described. By considering the appropriateness of the language used and the way these manifestations of God’s presence are described, we will establish a foundation based on actual facts for correctly understanding these appearances. 

I believe this is a better foundation than uncertain guesses built on long-standing prejudices. These prejudices have become so old that they are considered too respectable to ignore, even though they originally arose from a misunderstanding of the style and language of Scripture, or from a lack of careful attention when comparing various biblical passages on this subject. In my view, both of these factors have contributed significantly to making this subject obscure.

# SECTION I.

### The Divine Appearance to our First Parents in Paradise.

The first passage I will begin with contains a very early mention of a divine appearance while our first parents were still in Paradise <note>original: "Paradise"; the Garden of Eden</note>, found in Genesis 3:8: *And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day; and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden.* It is argued in many ways that this was a special divine appearance, specifically what is meant by the *Shekinah* <note>original: "Shechinah"; the visible manifestation of God's presence</note>.

First, it is described as an appearance of the Lord God. The "voice" they heard was "the Voice of the Lord God" <note>original Hebrew: קול יהוה אלהים (Kol Jehovah Elohim)</note>. The Septuagint <note>original: "70"; the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this as "the Voice of the Lord God" <note>original Greek: Της Φωνης του κυριου του θεου (Tes Phones tou kyriou tou theou)</note>. Onkelos <note>an influential ancient translator of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> translates it as "the Voice of the Word of the Lord" <note>original Aramaic: קל ממרא דיי (Kol Mimra D'Adonai); "Mimra" or "Word" was often used to describe God’s active presence</note>. These are expressions that seem to indicate a literal divine appearance—just as much a divine appearance as any other mentioned in the Bible. This is because "the Lord God," "the Word of the Lord," and "the Lord the God" are some of the highest and most specific titles for God in the language of the Scriptures and ancient paraphrases.

Furthermore, we can see another expression here that is equivalent to the *Shekinah* (which, as we have already seen, is used as a name for it): and that is, *the presence of God*. The text says: *And Adam and*

...and his *wife* hid themselves from the *presence* of the *Lord God* <note>original Hebrew: מפני יהוה אלהים (mippeni Jehovah Elohim)</note>. The Septuagint <note>original: 70; the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this as *from the face of the Lord God* <note>original Greek: απο προσωπο κυριο το Θεο (apo prosopo kyrio to Theo)</note>. Onkelos <note>an influential ancient translator of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> translates it as *from before the Lord* <note>original Aramaic: מן קדם ד׳ (Min Kodam Adonai)</note>. Of these, the Vulgate Latin <note>original: V. L.</note> provides a good sense: *from the face of the Lord God* <note>original Latin: a Facie Domini Dei</note>. All of these expressions are usually used to describe God’s glorious appearance in majesty, or the *Shekinah* <note>original: Shechinah; the visible manifestation of God’s presence</note>. But besides this evidence, the circumstances of the appearance itself will further confirm that this was a proper divine appearance.

How then is this appearance represented? *And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden, in the cool of the day.* Our translation does not, I think, give us as clear a notion of this appearance as is necessary for a just and distinct conception of it.

The *Voice of Jehovah*. This, says the learned Ainsworth <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622), a prominent English scholar and clergyman</note> on this passage, signifies any noise or sound, as in Ezekiel 1:24: *And when they went, the living creatures in the prophetic vision, I heard the noise of their wings, like the noise of great waters, as the voice of the Almighty, the voice of speech, as the noise of a host*; or rather, as the noise of a tumult. That expression is translated in this way in Jeremiah 11:16. The same word, as that learned man observes, is translated in Exodus 9:28 as *mighty thunderings* <note>original Hebrew: קלות אלהים (Koloth Elohim); literally "voices of God," as noted in the margin</note>. Such seems to be the proper interpretation of it in this place.

### Walking in the Garden.

This may also refer, says Henry Ainsworth <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622) was an influential English scholar and clergyman known for his meticulous translations of the Hebrew Bible</note>, to the "Voice," which is said to "walk" or "go on" when it increases in volume. For example, in Exodus 19:19: *And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and grew louder and louder* <note>original Hebrew: קול הולך (Kol holach), literally "a walking voice"</note>. This means the voice or sound of the trumpet "walked" or moved forward to a greater length, or increased and grew stronger; the word is used this way in many other places in the Bible.

Therefore, in this manifestation, we have a description of the presence of the Lord God <note>original Hebrew: *Jehovah Elohim*</note>, ushered in with a sound that moved and advanced through the Garden of Eden, coming closer and closer to our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note>. They, in turn, sought to hide themselves from the approaching appearance of the divine presence.

The general idea of this appearance can be accurately described using the words of Bishop Simon Patrick <note>Simon Patrick (1626–1707) was the Bishop of Ely and a prominent theologian</note>: "And they heard the sound of the majestic presence, or the glory of the Lord, approaching nearer and nearer to the place where they were." He notes that it is clear from this that there was a manifestation of an extraordinary presence. He adds, "I cannot help but think the *Shekinah* <note>original: Shechinah; the visible manifestation of God’s glory</note>, or divine majesty, appeared quite differently than it had before." This means it was not the gentle glow they had first known, but a more terrifying, burning light, as if it were about to consume them.

It suggests that after the Fall, the Shekinah appeared as a terrifying, burning light rather than the gentle radiance Adam and Eve had previously known.</summary>

## SECTION II.

### To *ABRAHAM*.

The next specific instance of a divine appearance I will consider is the appearance to *Abraham* in Genesis 17. This provides an example of the divine appearances during the patriarchal era. *First*, that the person appearing was *Jehovah*, just as in the earlier appearance to our first parents <note>Referring to Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden</note>.

*Secondly*, that in this appearance, he takes upon himself the character of Almighty God. According to the account of the text, this flame of fire which *Moses* saw seems—in the most natural and simple interpretation of the description—to be a fire in the middle of a bush. It appeared to *Moses* as a natural fire, which he expected would burn up and consume the bush. *Moses* does not describe anything miraculous about the flame or fire itself; rather, what caused him to wonder was that the bush was not burned.

When he turned to examine it more closely and to consider it as something extraordinary, his goal was to find the reason why the bush was not being destroyed: *And Moses said, "I will turn aside and see this great sight—why the bush is not burned."* This is all that I believe the description in this passage of Scripture allows us to determine regarding the nature of the flame *Moses* saw or how he saw it. At the very least, it does not allow us to assign any additional form or quality to the flame or fire beyond this specific detail: that it appeared as a natural fire—perhaps very strong and burning intensely—in the middle of a bush. Yet, even though it seemed certain to consume it, the bush remained unburned.

That it was a true appearance of *Jehovah Elohim*, or that special manifestation called the *Shechinah* <note>The *Shechinah* refers to the visible or perceptible manifestation of God's presence among humanity.</note>, presented in a perceptible manner.

Regarding the form of the appearance, it is described as a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. I see no reason, says Bishop **Patrick** <note>Simon Patrick (1626–1707), an influential English theologian and Bishop of Ely.</note>, to think there were two different clouds, since one and the same would serve both purposes; that is, the same pillar appeared like fire at night which looked like a cloud during the day. This seems to be suggested by **Moses** himself in Exodus, chapter 14, verse 20: *“And it, the pillar, came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel; and it was a cloud and darkness to them, the Egyptians, but it gave light by night to those, the Israelites, so that the one came not near the other all the night.”*

That is, as Mr. **Ainsworth** <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622), a renowned Hebrew scholar and non-conformist minister.</note> observes from the **Jerusalem** Targum, the cloud was half light and half darkness. The light gave light to **Israel**, and the

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the miraculous cloud that guided the Israelites during the Exodus, focusing on its appearance and the linguistic meaning of the word "pillar."</meta>

# An ESSAY on

It gave darkness to the **Egyptians**. One side of it was light, and the other was dark; like a thick cloud enlightened on one side where the sun shines strongly, but dark on the opposite side where the sun cannot pierce through it. Such a pillar of cloud and fire may the same cloud be on its different sides, and it becomes either one simply by changing the dark or light side for the other.

As it is called *a pillar of cloud*, and *a pillar of fire*, its form is usually supposed to be something like a column or a pillar in a building. I suppose, says Bishop **Patrick**, that it appeared from heaven in the form of a great, long pillar which spread itself out below and covered the entire host of **Israel**. But if this word is an allusion to the columns or pillars of architecture, the length of the pillar—in any proportion to such a base—must have been prodigious. Now, as Mr. **Ainsworth** remarks, a "pillar" in **Hebrew** is named for *standing up* or *stability*. <note>The Hebrew word for pillar is *amud* (עמוד), derived from the root *amad* (עמד), meaning "to stand."</note> Here, the term is applied by comparison to the cloud and fire that stood over the host of **Israel**. This would satisfy the original word, *amud* (עמוד), from the root *amad* (עמד), meaning "he stood" or "he remained," <note>original Latin: *stetit, mansit*</note> regardless of what particular form or shape the cloud standing over **Israel** might have had. It is therefore translated by the **Septuagint** <note>The "LXX," an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in several places as *Station* <note>original Greek: Στασις (*Stasis*); original Latin: *Statio*</note> as well as *Column* <note>original Greek: Στυλος (*Stylos*); original Latin: *Columna*</note>, and is used to describe the ordinary attendance of servants, or the proper place or station of the priests.

The ministers of the Temple, or the people; and it is accordingly translated by our translators as an *attendant place*, or proper station <gloss>a</gloss>, as in 1 *Kings* 10:5 and *Nehemiah* 9:3. In this sense, the word *pillar* would not so much describe the shape of the cloud as its stationary presence. The description may be explained in this way: And *Jehovah* went before them—the *Israelites*—in a stationary cloud that accompanied them, to lead them on their way. 

Indeed, the specific form of the cloud appears much closer to the form of a natural cloud, spread over a large part of the sky, than to a pillar of inconceivable height reaching up toward the heavens. For, as it is expressed by the Psalmist in *Psalm* 105:39: *He spread a cloud for a covering*. # THE SHECHINAH <note>Hebrew: "dwelling" or "settling"; the visible manifestation of the presence of God.</note>

Although I do not intend to investigate at length at this time the sense in which this appearance is described as *the Voice of Jehovah* and as *an Angel speaking*, I think it is a proper opportunity to briefly mention the two principal interpretations.

"...into the appearance of a flame by a certain spirit, like a trumpet, it was heard articulately by all, whether near or further away" <note>original Latin: "in flammæ speciem spiritu quodam, instar Tubæ, articulate ab omnibus audiretur, vel prope, vel longius distantibus."</note>. The way Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD) was a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> expresses himself is far from making it clear that he intended for the phrase "rational soul" <note>original Greek: "ψυχη λογικη" (psychē logikē)</note> to mean a proper angel or a separate spirit. This is because both the words "soul" and "reason" <note>original: "ψυχη" (psychē) and "λογος" (logos)</note> are used in very different senses throughout his writings.

In his treatise *On the Creation of the World* <note>original Latin title: "de Mundi Opificio"</note>, these terms are used to mean natural generative virtues and powers (page 7) or, according to his philosophy, "plastic powers" <term>plastic powers: in older philosophy, these are formative or creative forces capable of shaping matter into specific forms.</term>. These are very different from separate spirits or "demons" <note>original: "Dæmons." In the Greek context used by Philo, "demons" referred to spiritual beings or mediators, not necessarily evil spirits.</note>. Philo himself observes in his work *On Dreams* <note>original: "De Somniis," p. 455</note> that, according to the language of philosophy, this is the same as what the Scriptures call "angels."

It is remarkable that what Philo calls a "rational soul" here is the same thing he had described just before as God "having commanded an invisible sound to be created in the air" <note>original Greek: "κελευσας ηχην αορατον εν αερι δημιουργηθηναι" (keleusas ēchēn aoraton en aeri dēmiourgēthēnai)</note>. As much of a follower of Plato <note>original: "Platonist"</note> as Philo was, he seems here to allude to the Jewish notion that—just as the *Shekhinah* was a newly formed or created light, according to Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a highly influential Torah scholar and philosopher.</note>—so the "Voice from Heaven" was a newly formed or created voice. 

Philo seems to call it a "rational soul" because it shaped the air into a more distinct, clear, and harmonious sound than even the best-formed human organs of speech could produce. This was accomplished by some active principle or formative power <note>original: "plastic Form"</note> then produced by the power of God. It was not the proper act of some "demon" or separate intelligence, ac- <meta>catchword: according</meta>

Justin Martyr <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) was an early Christian philosopher and apologist who sought to bridge the gap between Greek philosophy and Christian doctrine.</note> and some other philosophical Fathers of the early Church understand the word *Angel* to mean the *Logos* <note>original Greek: "λόγος." Whether this was the meaning intended by *Philo*, and—more importantly—which of these views reflects the true meaning of the Scriptures, will be considered more effectively later. # THE SHECHINAH.

It may not be out of place here to observe the sentiments of the Jewish Church, as they are stated in the Jewish Creed. After the first article, which teaches the existence of a God who is the Creator and Governor of all things, the second article expresses the Divine Unity in this way: "I believe with perfect faith that the Creator, whose name is blessed, is uniquely one, with a unity that has no equal or similarity at all, and that he alone has been, is, and will be our God." <note>original Latin: "Fide perfecta credo, Creatorem, cujus nomen benedictum, unicum esse, Unitate quae nullam omnino similem habeat, illumque solum Deum nostrum fuisse, esse, et futurum esse."</note> And from this, the Creed—as well as Moses—infers the unity of worship; <margin>Buxtorf, *The Jewish Synagogue* <note>original: "Buxtorf in Jud." refers to Johannes Buxtorf's *Synagoga Judaica*, a famous 17th-century study of Jewish customs.</note></margin> for the fifth article is expressed thus: "I believe with perfect faith that the Creator alone, whose name is blessed, is to be worshiped, and no one besides him." <note>original Latin: "Fide perfecta credo, solum Creatorem, cujus nomen benedictum, et neminem praeterea adorandum esse."</note>

I shall just add the observation of Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>: "The second foundation is the Unity of God: namely, that He, who is the cause of all things, is one; yet not as one in a general category or species, or as a single composite individual that is divided into many units; nor as a simple body, one in number, which is capable of division and distribution into infinite parts; but that He is one with a unity to which there is no other similar in any way. And this is the second foundation, which is indicated by his own word: *Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one.*" <note>original Latin: "Fundamentum secundum est Unitas Dei : scil : Illum, qui omnium causa est, unum esse ; non tamen ut unum genere, vel specie, vel ut individuum unum compositum, quod in unitates multas dividitur ; vel ut corpus simplex, unum numero, quod divisionis et distributionis in partes infinitas capax est ; verum eum unum esse unitate, cui non sit alia aliqua ullo modo similis. Atque hoc est fundamentum secundum, quod indicatur dicto ipsius : Audi, Israel, Dominus Deus tuus unus est."</note> *The Gate of Moses* <note>original: "Porta Mosis," a collection of Maimonides's writings edited by Edward Pococke in 1655.</note>, pages 165, 166. Regarding the fifth fundamental article of the Jewish Creed, Maimonides gives this account: "The fifth foundation: that He is the one who must be worshiped, and whose veneration and obedience are to be proclaimed; and this must not be offered to any of those things that are inferior to Him in essence, such as the Angels..." <note>original Latin: "Fundamentum quintum, Illum esse qui colendus sit, cujusque veneratio et obsequium praedicanda ; neque hoc alicui Eorum, qui ipso essentia inferiora sunt, Angelorum..."</note>

In this passage, the "Place of the Habitation" is also called, in verses 19 and 20, *a house built for the Name, or to the Name of the Lord God of Israel.* This is equivalent to the expression in verse 16: *to build a house so that my Name might be in it.* 

This suggests to us that the inner sanctuary <term>original: "Oracle"</term> and the Name of Jehovah, being placed in the Temple, are expressions equivalent to the "Habitation of the Divine Majesty," or the "Presence of the Glory," or the *Shechinah* <term>the visible manifestation of God’s presence</term>. This justifies the paraphrase written by Onkelos <note>a famous translator of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> on Deuteronomy 12:5: *The place which the Lord shall choose to put his Name there.* Onkelos translates this as, "to cause my Shechinah to dwell there" <note>original Aramaic: לאשראה שכינתי, *Leashraah Schechinti*</note>, as we observed before in Chapter 7, section 4. 

God himself seems to explain this expression in the same way in 1 Kings 9:3 <note>The original OCR text cites 1 Kings 19:3, but the quote is from 1 Kings 9:3</note>: *I have consecrated this house which you have built, to put my Name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there perpetually.* These words—*my eyes and my heart shall be there perpetually*—strongly declare the divine presence. As we can see, they are equivalent to God "putting his Name" there.

### CHAPTER III.
#### *The Prophetic Representations of the* SHECHINAH.

In this way, we have followed the account of these divine appearances down to the full establishment of the Hebrew Church and the state of religion and worship under the Temple. ## CHAPTER III.

### The Prophetical Representations of the SHECHINAH.

Up to this point, we have traced these divine appearances <note>original: "Appearances"; likely referring to theophanies, or visible manifestations of God</note> to the full establishment of the *Hebrew Church* and the state of religion and worship under the Temple. However, it may give us even more insight into this subject to consider the prophetic descriptions of these same appearances, or the presence of *Jehovah* in his Temple. We should also consider the prophetic descriptions of that same divine presence after the first Temple was destroyed, and during the time the second Temple lacked <note>original: "wanted"</note> the *Shechinah* or Glory; this continued until, at last, this second Temple was blessed with the most glorious of all *Shechinah* manifestations in the presence of the King *Messiah* <note>original: "Messias"</note>.

# SECTION I.
## Concerning ISAIAH.

The first appearance of this kind that I would like to consider is the representation of the divine Presence to the Prophet Isaiah in chapter six. In this, we have a very instructive account of how the Presence of God in His Temple was understood by the Hebrew Church, and how it was represented in prophetic style and language.

The year in which King Uzziah died, when Isaiah had this vision, occurred near the middle of the period of time between the building of Solomon’s Temple and its eventual destruction. This vision does not represent the Shechinah <note>original: "Schechinah"</note> in its usual, fixed residence within the Most Holy Place <term>The Holy of Holies, the innermost sanctuary of the Temple where the Ark of the Covenant was kept</term>, but as having come out from there and sitting upon a throne—probably, as most interpreters believe, on the porch or portico of the Temple. 

Thus, the throne was elevated on high, but the "train" <note>The trailing part of a royal robe or a ceremonial covering for a throne of state</note> fell down so as to reach within the Temple and cover the entire view of it: *I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.* Above it, surrounding the Shechinah seated upon the throne, stood the Seraphim <note>original: "Seraphims"</note>, the angels who serve as ministers and attendants to the divine Presence; and one cried out to another and said:

### CHAPTER III.

#### *The Prophetic Representations of the* SHECHINAH <note>original: "SCHECHINAH"</note>.

In the previous chapters, we have traced the appearances of God up to the full establishment of the Hebrew Church and the state of religion and worship under the Temple. However, it may provide further insight into this subject to consider the prophetic representations of these same appearances, or the presence of Jehovah in his Temple. 

We will also examine the prophetic depictions of that same divine presence after the first Temple was destroyed, and during the time when the second Temple lacked the Shechinah <note>original: "Schechinah"</note> or Glory. This continued until, eventually, this later house was blessed with the most glorious of all Shechinahs in the presence of the King Messiah <note>original: "Messias"</note>.

## Concerning ISAIAH.

The first appearance of this kind I would like to consider is the representation of the divine presence to the prophet Isaiah in Chapter 6. In this, we have a very instructive account of how the Hebrew Church understood the presence of God in his Temple, and how it was represented in prophetic style <note>original: "Stile"</note> and language.

The year in which King Uzziah died—which was when Isaiah had this vision—was nearly at the midpoint of the time between the building of Solomon's Temple and its destruction. ## SECTION II.

### Regarding EZEKIEL.

To proceed: The prophecy of *Ezekiel* provides such a representation of the divine appearance as deserves particular attention.

The *Jewish Masters* <note>The rabbinic sages and scholars of Jewish law and tradition.</note> call this prophecy the *Merkavah* <note>original: "Mercavah"; Hebrew for "chariot," referring to the throne-chariot of God in Ezekiel's vision.</note> and suppose it to contain their mystical and secret theology, which in their opinion is not lawful to explain. For this reason, it seems that everything *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a highly influential Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> says about it in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Nebochim"; Maimonides' most famous philosophical work.</note>, Part 3, is very mystical and obscure.

Whatever mystical and secret meaning the vision may be supposed to have, what specifically relates to our purpose appears, I think, quite plain and in conformity with the other divine appearances.

The prophet himself calls the appearance (Ezekiel 1:28) *the appearance of the likeness of the glory of Jehovah*. That is, it describes the manner in which the *Shekhinah* <note>The dwelling or settling divine presence of God.</note> appeared to the prophet, the description of which is briefly this:

The heavens were opened to *Ezekiel* in a vision by the River *Chebar* (verse 1). *A whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the color of amber, out of the midst*

Thus, we have seen the representations of the Glory of the God of Israel, or the *Shekhinah*, during the time the Temple was standing. Although some of Ezekiel's visions occurred a short time after the destruction of the Temple—as the prophecy in chapter 33 was given after he had received news <note>original: "Advice"</note> that the city had been taken (verse 21)—these prophecies can still be considered as referring to the Temple while it stood. This is because the principal vision, and the Glory departing and returning, are designed to express the manner in which the *Shekhinah* dwelled there.

## SECTION III.

### TO DANIEL.

The visions of Daniel are the first to be noticed in this period, and so I will proceed to them.

Daniel, a member of the royal family of Judah, was a captive but was educated in the imperial palace of Babylon. He had a dream, or vision, in the first year of Belshazzar (Chapter 7), about twenty-nine years after the capture of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar. This representation is somewhat different from any we have encountered so far.

<margin>Lowth on this passage <note>Refers to William Lowth, a prominent 17th-century biblical commentator</note>.</margin>
"*I watched*," says the prophet in verse 9, "*until the thrones were cast down*"—or rather, until the thrones were set down, pitched, or placed. "When the thrones were set" <note>original Greek: Ὅτε οἱ θρόνοι ἐτέθησαν</note>, according to the Septuagint <note>The "70"; an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>. "Until the thrones were placed" <note>original Latin: donec throni positi sunt</note>, according to the Vulgate <note>V. L.</note>. This is the correct meaning of the original word, as it is used by the Chaldean <term>Chaldee</term> Paraphrast <note>An Aramaic translator or commentator on the Hebrew Bible</note> in Jeremiah 1:15.

> When the thrones were thus set or placed, the prophet beheld, and the *Ancient of Days* sat down, whose *garment* was white as *snow*, and the *hair* of his *head* like *fine wool*. *His throne* was like a *fiery flame*, and his *wheels* as *burning fire*. *A fiery stream* issued and came *forth from before him. The judgment was set, and the books were opened.* <note>This passage is from the biblical Book of Daniel, chapter 7, verses 9–10.</note>

It is not very relevant to our current purpose to consider which specific judgment is being discussed here. What concerns us is the manner of the representation, or how the *Shekhinah* <note>original: "Scheckinah"; a Hebrew term referring to the settled presence or glory of God.</note> appeared. I believe this is clearly intended as a description of it, and the Person is represented as the universal Lord and Judge of all. It appears to represent the Divine Presence, not as if in a temple or a palace (for the temple was destroyed at that time); rather, it expresses the solemnity of a session of justice <note>In this context, a "session of justice" refers to a formal sitting of a high court.</note>. In this description, there are some things to consider regarding the representation of the Person, and some regarding his seat of justice. 

With respect to the Person, who is called the *Ancient of Days*—most interpreters agree that this title is intended to express eternity and to describe God as the first of beings and the origin of all other beings. We may under<unclear>st</unclear>and it as a description of *Jehovah*, who speaks of himself in this way in *Isaiah 43:12, 13.*

*You are my Witnesses, says the Lord, that I am God.—Yes, before the day was, I am he.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 43:12-13.</note> Daniel’s expression, *Athik Jomin* <note>original Aramaic: עתיק יומין</note>, may, I think, be translated as *more ancient than Time* <sup>a</sup>, as well as the *Ancient of Days*. ***

<sup>a</sup> The Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldee"; the language used in parts of the Book of Daniel.</note> words are hardly capable of the interpretation the learned author would fix on them, namely, *More ancient than Time*. The word *Athik* <note>original: עתיק</note> signifies what is so ancient as to be permanent, durable, and liable to no variation and decay. *With me are durable riches* <note>original: הון עתק (Hon Attek)</note>, as we translate the words in *Proverbs* 8:18. Riches long laid up, inviolable and undecaying. And the *Ancient of Days* is that ancient, eternal, and immutable Being, on whom no days or years can make any alteration or change whatever. See Mr. Schultens <note>Albert Schultens (1686–1750), a Dutch philologist and orientalist.</note> on *Proverbs* 8:18, and it is parallel to the Psalmist’s description of God in *Psalm* 102:27, 28, etc.

> *...given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, so that all people, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom is that which shall not be destroyed.* <note>Quoting Daniel 7:14.</note>

It is surely a very strange idea of Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian known for his historical—rather than purely prophetic—interpretations of the Bible.</note> that by "one like the Son of Man" is meant the Roman people without a king. "The Roman people having no king among themselves, as it is said in 1 Maccabees 8:14. Sons of men are called private citizens, as in Psalm 82:7 <note>original: "Populus Romanus nullum habens intra se Regem, ut dicitur, 1 Macchab. viii. 14. Filii hominum dicuntur privati, ut Psalm, lxxxii. 7."</note>," says Grotius on this passage. He allows, indeed, that this Roman people was a clear representation of Christ: "Moreover, the Roman people is no obscure image of Christ <note>original: "Est autem Populus Romanus non obscure Christi Imago."</note>." 

But how can the Roman people ever be said to come with the "clouds of heaven"? Or how could the Roman people, without a king, receive a kingdom which shall not be destroyed, when the liberties and power of Rome were both lost under the Imperial government? This is especially true since it seems this definitive sentence was intended to set a fixed end to Roman power, as the power of the "fourth beast" is most probably intended to mean the power of the Romans (see verse 7).

The everlasting kingdom spoken of here clearly seems to refer to the kingdom of the Messiah <note>original: "Messias"</note>, which was to last forever. "Coming in the clouds of heaven"—to use the words of a learned author—is a known symbol of heaven, and of divine power and majesty.

I shall only, therefore, make one observation: that on the assumption that this was the Shekinah <note>original: "Schechinah"; the visible manifestation of the presence of God</note>, it comes very close to a human form. This was possibly to suggest that as in time the Shekinah was to appear in human nature, so the very form of the Shekinah—differing from that under the first temple—should serve to prepare the minds of people for such a Shekinah as was to be manifested in the days of the Messiah, the King. As the fullness of the Godhead was to dwell in him bodily, he was to be the greater glory of the second temple and the more perfect Shekinah of all later times.

### SECTION IV.
## To ZECHARIAH.

To proceed: I come now to consider another representation in the prophecy of *Zechariah*. This is the last I shall examine in the Old Testament, being written just before prophecy and prophetic vision ended in the Church until the appearance of the *Messiah*.

Both of these interpretations appear, in some respects, preferable to each other; and yet both are subject to great difficulties and lack the consistency needed to make the representation of this vision fully uniform, clear, and intelligible.

The supposition of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a prominent Dutch jurist and theologian</note> that *Michael* addressed *Jehovah* seems to be a mistake. This is because the answer of *Jehovah* to that address is explicitly credited to the angel who talked with the prophet and who gave the command to the prophet in verses 13 and 14, as we observed earlier. So, while *Grotius* seems to have judged correctly that this address was made to *Jehovah*, it was not, however, the address of the *Man between the Myrtle Trees* (whom he identifies as *Michael*), but rather the address of the "Angel Interpreter." Therefore, on this point, the interpretation of Mr. *Lowth* <note>William Lowth (1660–1732), an English theologian and father of Bishop Robert Lowth; he wrote well-regarded commentaries on the prophets</note>—who assumes the address was made by the angel who talked with *Zechariah* and that the answer was given to him—seems preferable to the interpretation by *Grotius*.

But on the other hand, as we also observed before, Mr. *Lowth* seems to have made a mistake when he assumes that the Angel Interpreter addresses his prayer to the *Man between the Myrtle Trees* as the *Logos* <note>Greek for "the Word," referring to the pre-incarnate Son of God</note>, using the title of *Lord of Hosts*; and that this *Man between the Myrtle Trees* was the *Jehovah* who answered him.

# CONCLUSION.

*Containing some observations on the preceding appearances of the Shekinah, to explain its intentions and uses.*

The appearances which we have considered not only lead to some knowledge of a great part of the Mosaic <note>original: *Moſaical*; relating to Moses and the laws given at Mount Sinai</note> revelation of religion and of the worship of the Church in that state, but they are also the principal manifestations of God's presence from the beginning of revelation until the times of Moses. It is worth our serious inquiry what might be the intention of these manifestations and what uses they were designed for; for we may well suppose them worthy of the wisdom and goodness of God, who chose thus to manifest himself to the Church, and that some blessings were designed by them suitable to such condescension—

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page, starting with the word "condescension" to describe God’s voluntary act of manifesting himself to humanity.</meta>

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>THE SHEKINAH</header>

condescension, which it will be useful to understand correctly.

The state of religion, specifically according to the revelation given by Moses—and especially the nature of the divine appearance in the Shekinah <note>original: *Schechinah*; the dwelling or settled presence of God</note>—was also a symbolic representation, or a sketch, of the most perfect state of religion according to the revelation of Jesus Christ. <margin>Hebrews 10:1; Colossians 2:17</margin> As the scripture says, *the Law has a shadow of good things to come*. A correct understanding of the true spiritual meaning of the Mosaic state of religion (which represents and outlines the Gospel dispensation <term>dispensation: a divine system or era of religious order</term>) will help clarify our knowledge of both. The close relationship between the two is a point of more profitable instruction than is commonly realized.

...was expressed in whatever way <note>original Latin: "cunque exprimebatur"</note>: the <term>Cherubim</term> were not images of God, like <note>original: "as"</note> **Jeroboam's** calves <note>Two golden calves set up by King Jeroboam I in the 10th century BCE, often cited as a cautionary tale of idolatry</note>, nor were they images of any specific angel. Instead, they were emblems by which the angelic nature was expressed in some way.

If we consider the form of the <term>Cherubim</term> in the Temple based on the description of the <term>Cherubim</term> in the Book of **Ezekiel**, or from the four beasts (or rather, "living creatures") in the Book of **Revelation**, we find a composite form made of a man, a lion, an eagle, and an ox. This specific arrangement of hands, wings, and feet seems clearly designed to teach us that these <term>Cherubim</term> were not intended to be the likeness of any actual creature. Rather, they served as an emblem to represent the distinguished qualities of the beings they were meant to symbolize. Thus, while the glorious light of the <term>Shekhinah</term> <note>original: "Schechinah"</note> represented the majesty of God’s presence, the form of the <term>Cherubim</term> represented the knowledge and power of angels, who are the highest beings next to God. In the words of a great author:

<margin>
John Spencer, 
*On the Ritual Laws of the Hebrews* 
<note>original: "Leg. Heb."</note> 
book 3, chapter 5, 
section 5.
</margin>
> *The greatest knowledge and power of angels, second only to God.* <note>original Latin: "Summam, secundum Deum, scientiam et potentiam Angelorum."</note>

Therefore, the might of a lion, the strength and useful labor of an ox, the wisdom and prudence of a man, and the keen sight, swiftness, and activity of an eagle are very fitting and significant emblems of the knowledge and power that are attributed to the angels of God.

In the solemn service of this day, we clearly perceive a design to instruct the worshippers and keep in their memory such important principles of true religion as these:

That *Jehovah*, whose presence in the most holy place of the Temple made it a sanctuary and place of solemn worship, was himself a *proper object of worship*, to whom the Church was to direct and offer all prayers, praises, confessions, gifts, and sacrifices. It showed that *Jehovah alone* was their God, and they were to have no other besides him, nor acknowledge any other by any religious act.

# THE SHEKHINAH

<margin>Idolatry.</margin> The institutions of the *Hebrew* Church and nation, and therefore its religious and political structures <note>original: "Constitutions"</note>, are clearly designed for this: to lead and keep them in acknowledgment of *Jehovah*, the God who brought them out of *Egypt* and out of the "house of bondage," as the one true God, and to *have no other gods before Him*. This was the first article of the covenant between God and them, which was stored within the Ark of the Testimony. The Ark was covered by the Mercy Seat, over which dwelt the *Shekhinah* <note>original: "Schechinah"</note>, or the glory of the presence of *Jehovah*.

The purpose <note>original: "Use"</note> of the *Shekhinah* will appear even more clearly if we examine the chief principles of the idolatry of their neighboring nations, by which the knowledge of the one true God was so corrupted that it was almost lost. The principles of idolatry consisted mainly of the notions people had received regarding certain beings of high spiritual and angelic natures. Although these beings were far inferior to the supreme God, they were still far superior to the spirits of mortal men and to their own souls. In this regard, there was universal evidence <note>original: "Attestation"</note> for the doctrine of angels and distinct spirits. People added the departed souls of great men to the ranks of the gods and worshipped them as *heroes*, or gods of a lower order than the angels—those immortal gods who had never been embodied or lived in human flesh. ## the Evils of Life, and the Continuance and Increase of every Blessing.

Finally, in the washings, purifications, clothing <note>original: "Habits"</note>, and actions of the entire Temple service and worship performed before this *Shekhinah* <note>the visible manifestation of God’s presence</note>, you have a plain and strong indication of the purity of heart and true holiness that were expected of the worshipers of *Jehovah*. It showed what profound respect <note>original: "awful Respect"</note> and religious reverence was required of everyone who approached His presence.

This appearance of *Jehovah* through His *Shekhinah* is of such excellent use because it teaches, settles, and confirms—through specific revelation and express instruction—the principal truths of religion. It explains and establishes the chief doctrines that the "light of nature" <note>the knowledge of God accessible through human reason and the natural world</note> taught concerning the perfections and will of God, as well as the nature, uses, and goals of His worship. At the same time, it guards against the prevailing idolatry of the world in such a way that, if this system of worship were observed even to a reasonable degree, it would effectively prevent or cure idolatry in both belief and practice.

The continued existence of the oracle—which was consulted by the high priest on occasions of great and public concern—served to give them courage and hope in all their endeavors, as they were under the direction of God through his oracle. This protected them from one great temptation and snare of idolatry: the curious and eager desire to know future events. In Philo's writings, published some time earlier, there were many things closely related to Christian doctrines. Consequently, there was some danger that people, captivated by *Philo’s* eloquence, might follow him too closely and blend the errors of his philosophy with the true doctrines of Christianity.

*Plato's philosophy* was held in high regard. He largely followed *Pythagoras* in his complex and metaphysical reasoning. He had introduced many elements from the doctrines of the *Egyptians*, the *Persian Magi*, the *Assyrians*, and the *Chaldeans*, and taught them in a way that was not easy to understand and was even easier to misinterpret. For *Plato*—in addition to the mysterious methods of *Egyptian* and *Pythagorean* teaching—very cautiously avoided giving offense by saying anything openly against the popular religion <note>original: "Theology"</note> of his country, which had proved so fatal to his master *Socrates*. These concerned "substantial emanations" <term>substantial emanations: The idea that divine beings or powers flow out from the essence of God like rays from the sun, rather than being created out of nothing.</term> from the Deity and certain angelic beings who were seen as the instruments of God for the formation of the world and the administration of providence. These ideas were very different from the Mosaic <note>Relating to Moses and the Old Testament.</note> and Christian doctrines of creation and providence. Yet many of these notions were adopted by *Philo*, and they were too well received by many Christians—some of good reputation—in the early days of Christianity.

Some time before the writing of this Gospel, there were also people claiming to have a greater understanding than is common, especially in areas of difficult science and more sublime philosophy. These were called the "Men of Knowledge," or *Gnostics* <term>Gnostics: From the Greek word *gnosis* (knowledge). A group of early thinkers who believed in secret, mystical knowledge as the path to salvation.</term>. They centered a great part of their supposed higher knowledge on various "genealogies" and "conjunctions," which they viewed as substantial emanations from the Deity. They spoke of them in a manner so far beyond all understanding that they were bound to confuse anyone who listened to them. They were very likely to lead people away from the simplicity of Christian revelation and into either mysterious nonsense or dangerous errors.

According to the Gnostics, that "Word" and "Life" were a couple of *Aeons* <term>original: "Æons"; in Gnosticism, these are divine emanations or spiritual beings that inhabit the realm of light</term> emitted from two other *Aeons*, namely *Mind* (also called the *Only Begotten*) and *Truth*. *St. John*, on the contrary, teaches that the several characters of *Life, Light, Grace, Truth*, and *Only Begotten* all belong to the *Word made flesh* and center in his person. He teaches that he was not emitted from any intermediate *Aeons* of recent time, nor produced in a different place outside of the *Pleroma* <term>original: "Pleroma"; the Greek word for "fullness," referring to the totality of divine powers and the dwelling place of the supreme God</term>, to which the dwelling of the supreme God was most absurdly confined by the *Gnostics*.
