...in whom *the Word* was made flesh; and that the glory of the Father appeared in the *Christ*; and that this *Word made flesh* was the same *Word* which in the beginning was with God, which was *God*, or, *God was the Word*.

But in order to understand this description more distinctly, it will be necessary to consider how *St. John* uses this expression, *the Word*; for by this, the doctrine which *St. John* teaches, and the true meaning and sense of his argument, will be best understood.

It would seem *St. John* did not intend to use this expression, *the Word*, or *Logos* <note>original: "$\lambda o\gamma o\varsigma$"; the Greek term for "Word," "Reason," or "Discourse"</note>, in the *Platonic* or *Gnostic* sense <note>Platonists and Gnostics used the term "Logos" to describe various intermediate spiritual beings or divine emanations; the author argues John is reclaiming the term</note>; it appears that he rather intended to oppose and censure their errors, and to preserve the Christian Church from falling into them.

It is much more likely that *St. John* chose this expression to explain the truth according to the doctrines of the ancient revelation and Church.

It is well known that the Oracle from which God spoke, or gave his Word, is called *Debir* <note>original: "דביר"; the Hebrew term for the "Holy of Holies" or the innermost sanctuary of the Temple</note>, from the word *Dabar* <note>original: "דבר"; the Hebrew verb meaning "to speak" or the noun for "word"</note>, which signifies to *speak*. In the same way, the *Greek word* *Logion* <note>original: "$\lambda o\gamma\iota o\nu$"; meaning a divine utterance, oracle, or scripture</note>, or Oracle, expresses the place from which the *Logos*, or *Word of God*, came. Now, as the Word of God is a revelation of God’s inward designs and purposes, or of the ends designed and plans formed by his infinite wisdom for the accomplishment of them; this expression...

[Ex]pression, *the Word*, or *Logos* <note>original: "$\lambda o\gamma o\varsigma$"</note>, will signify the inward purposes of God, according to the plans which his infinite wisdom has formed, and the *outward* revelation of those purposes by words. *Clement* of *Alexandria* observes, concerning the meaning of this expression: "That the Word of the Father of all things is not his word spoken, but the manifested wisdom and goodness of God, his almighty and truly divine power, or almighty will <note>original: "$\theta\epsilon\lambda\eta\mu\alpha \;\pi\alpha\nu\tau o\kappa\rho\alpha\tau o\rho\iota\kappa o\nu$" (thelema pantokratorikon)</note>." In another place, he seems to define this as the Idea in the divine mind, which, when put forth or brought into action, is the cause of all things. "An idea is a thought of God... and the Word, coming forth, is the cause of creation" <note>original: "$\mathrm{I}\delta\epsilon\alpha \;\epsilon\nu\nu o\eta\mu\alpha \;\tau o\upsilon \;\Theta\epsilon o\upsilon \dots \pi\rho o\epsilon\lambda\theta\omega\nu \;\delta\epsilon \;\omicron \;\lambda o\gamma o\varsigma \;\delta\eta\mu\iota o\upsilon\rho\gamma\iota\alpha\varsigma \;\alpha\iota\tau\iota o\varsigma$"</note>.

The word *Logos* <note>original: "$\lambda o\gamma o\varsigma$"</note> is in a similar manner often translated into *Latin* as *Ratio* (Reason), *Sermo* (Speech), or *Verbum* (Word); and it is often understood sometimes in the one sense, and sometimes in the other. Sometimes it signifies the ideas, the exemplars, and the patterns in the divine mind, according to which the supreme Father of all had purposed to make and to govern all things. This seems to be much the same as what was meant by the *all-governing will* <note>original: "$\theta\epsilon\lambda\eta\mu\alpha \;\pi\alpha\nu\tau o\kappa\rho\alpha\tau o\rho\iota\kappa o\nu$"</note> or the *Son* <note>original: "$\upsilon\iota o\varsigma$"</note>...

# The *LOGOS* Considered.

<margin>
*Conjectures on Heresies*,
pages 17, 18.
</margin>
While *Logos* is explained as "Speech" and "Word" <note>original: "*Sermonem* et *Verbum*"</note>, I would consider it to be taken here chiefly for that Word which mandates and commands. This is because the words *Amar* <note>Hebrew/Arabic for "to say/command"</note> and *Qawl* <note>Arabic for "voice/word"</note> are frequently found in that same sense among the Arabs, no less than *Medabber* <note>Hebrew for "speaking"</note> is among the Hebrews. So much so, that the *Logos* is like an *Emir* <note>An Arabic title for a commander or leader</note> to the Arabs, or like a "Dictator" <note>One who dictates or commands</note> to the Romans, a title which Varro <note>A Roman scholar</note> derives from a "saying" or a "command" <note>original: "*Dicto*, seu *Jussu*"</note>. In this sense, I believe the terms *Logos* and *Demiurge* <note>original: "δημιεργον" (Craftsman or Creator)</note> are frequently used for the same thing by the Platonists—especially *Philo*, who established the *Logos* as the creator and governor of all things. 

The theology of the Egyptians joined these two meanings of the *Logos* together. For so says Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note>: "The Creator Intellect <note>original: "*Opifex Intellectus*"</note>, who is both the Lord of Truth and of Wisdom—as he proceeds into the work of creation <note>original: "generationem"</note> and brings the hidden power of latent reasons into the light—is called *Amun* <note>original: "*Ammoun*"</note> in the Egyptian language. However, in as much as he performs all things without falsehood and skillfully along with Truth, he is named *Ptah* <note>original: "*Phtha*"</note>."

Upon which our Author further observes: "Thus, the *Logos* acts as the author of Oracles <note>original: "*logiwn Author*"</note>. Or he is that *Ammon*: if you look at the truth being spoken <note>original: "veritatem enunciatam"</note>, he is called *Amen*, from the Arabic *Amunah* <note>original: "אמונה"</note>, which is 'Truth,' or the Coptic *Amen*, which is 'True.' If you look at what is invisible and hidden <note>original: "$\alpha\phi\alpha\nu\eta$ (aphane) et $\kappa\epsilon\kappa\rho\upsilon\mu\mu\epsilon\nu\omicron\nu$ (kekrymmenon)"</note>, he is named *Ames*, according to what Plutarch taught us above. But in as much as the same Being proceeds to work and to act, he was called *Ptah*—from a word, I believe, related to the Arabic *Bara* <note>original: "ברא"</note>, which is to be the beginning and creator of a thing. And indeed even this name *Ptah*, as understood by the Egyptians—"

...was understood—it also connoted the Giver of the Oracle, the one who speaks the truth; since *Pata* <note>original: פתא</note> means "to give an answer." From this comes the name of the Muslim *Mufti* <note>original: מפת (Muphti); a Muslim legal expert who empowers laws by his word</note>; as if, to use the words of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, he were "a protector of truth and wisdom" <note>original: αληθειας και σοφιας προστατης</note>.

<margin>*Prideaux's Connection*, book 5, year 446.</margin> 
The counselors of Nebuchadnezzar are called this in the Hebrew of Daniel 3:28 and Daniel 4:33. Similarly, the Mishnaic doctors <note>Scholars of the Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> were called *Amoraim* <note>literally "those who say" or "speakers"</note> because they dictated the explanations of the Mishnah that are contained in the Gemara <note>The part of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis of the Mishnah</note>.

It may be further observed that the title *Imer* or *Amer*, both of which literally mean "the Word," signifies a Prince, Lord, or similar rank among the current Eastern nations. 
<margin>*Selden’s Titles of Honor*, vol. 3, pp. 193, 194.</margin> 
According to Mr. Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century legal scholar and polymath</note>, this title is given not only to their supreme princes but also to the lieutenants of provinces. Sampsates Spachanes, a Persian and Muslim living near the beginning of the Ottoman Empire, calls all of Turkey "the country of the great *Amir*" <note>original: την χωραν τυ μεγαλυ Αμηρα</note>—that is, the country of the great *Amir*, or *Word*.

The most ancient and most proper title is *Amir*—or *Emir—al-Mu'minin*. It signifies "Prince, Lord, or Emperor of the True Believers."

### The LOGOS Considered:

There is one passage that might be imagined to speak of the ascension of *Christ’s* body to where it was before: <margin>*John 6:62.*</margin> *What if you should see the Son of Man <note>A title Jesus frequently used for himself, emphasizing both his humanity and his role as the messianic figure from the Book of Daniel.</note> ascend up to where he was before?* 

As this seems to refer to the ascension of *Christ’s* body after the resurrection, which was to be visible in the sight of his disciples, it might also be thought to assert that he was in heaven before in his natural body, in the same manner in which they saw him ascend. However, the *Son of Man*, properly speaking, was made of a woman and born of the Virgin *Mary*; his visible body did not exist before his birth. 

If he was indeed in heaven before his ascension after the resurrection, it would make some earlier ascension of *Christ* necessary for various reasons. This would strongly support the theory mentioned earlier: that before he began his ministry, he was taken up into heaven to be fully instructed and informed about the nature and quality of his office, and the entire message he was to deliver to mankind. 

But as this theory is—as was observed before—without any historical foundation, why may it not be understood as a declaration of *Christ’s* divine and heavenly authority, commission, and instructions? He often used a figurative way of speaking, and his visible ascension in a short time would provide full evidence of that authority. It is as if he had said: "You will soon see me ascend visibly with my body into heaven, which

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how Christ, as the "Word made flesh," possessed a divine glory that he chose to set aside. It specifically examines the Greek term "Morphe" (form) to explain the transition from divine to human appearance.</meta>

<header>TEXTS of Scripture relating to the LOGOS considered.</header>

...how it would not have been an undeserved honor for him to have appeared with a dignity equal to any of the divine manifestations. However, in humility, he laid aside this glory and chose to live among us as a man, appearing to be in a state of subjection until he was exalted to the right hand of the throne of God. Then it was proclaimed that <margin>John 5:27</margin> the Father had given all power in heaven and earth to him, as he is—and because he is—the Son of Man, in whom the Word is made flesh.

There is a remarkable use among the Greek writers of the word *Morphe* <note>original: Μορφη</note>, which our translators have rendered as **the form of God**. In Greek literature, it signifies a character or an appearance. For example, in pagan <note>original: Heathen</note> theology, it refers to when a god laid aside the appearance and character of his divinity and took on the outward appearance of a man, or a human shape. Thus, it is said of *Bacchus*: 
<margin>Euripides, *The Bacchae*, Prologue</margin> 
"I, Dionysus, have changed my form from a god to that of a mortal." <note>original Greek: Διονυσος μορφην δ’ αμειψας εκ θεου βροτησιαν; Latin: *Atque ex Deo, humanam me induens in imaginem.*</note> This is further explained: "For this reason, I have taken a mortal appearance and transformed my shape into the nature of a man." <note>original Greek: Ων ενεκ’ ειδος θνητον αλλαξας εχω, μορφην τ’ εμην μετεβαλον εις ανδρος φυσιν; Latin: *Unde et Mortali sumpta imagine, me in ora, et habitum transformavi Viri.*</note>

In a similar way, the Romans used to describe the frequent appearances of their deities. When *Venus* appeared to her son <margin>Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 1</margin> *Aeneas*, she was described as "wearing the face and dress of a maiden." <note>original Latin: *Virginis Os habitumque gerens.*</note> Her son indeed addresses her as a goddess, but it was because of something...

It might be observed that among the Greeks, the terms *morphe* <note>original: μορφη — form</note>, *eidos* <note>original: ειδος — appearance</note>, and *physis* <note>original: φυσιϛ — nature</note> seem to be used in very nearly the same sense, and that the Romans copy them very closely. So, the phrase "Bearing the face and appearance of a maiden" <note>original Latin: *Virginis os habitumque gerens*</note> is directly opposed to the description "revealing herself as a goddess, just as she is seen by the inhabitants of heaven, and in her full stature." 
<margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 1, Fable 9.</margin>
And thus another author wrote: "And I, a god, travel the earth under a human image." <note>original Latin: *Et Deus humana lustro sub imagine terras.*</note> From these forms of expression, we may learn how to use these terms when they are applied to the different ways in which pagan <note>original: Heathen</note> theology supposed their gods to appear: whether as gods with the proper marks of their divinity (that is, in their own shape and proper dignity) or in a borrowed shape and form, with only the dignity and honors suited to the character they assumed.

<header>TEXTS of Scripture relating to</header>

But rather than dwelling on the views or language of pagan <note>original: "Heathen"</note> writers—though they may be useful for showing the proper meaning of several expressions, certainly much better than mere philosophical speculation—let us consider how the divine appearances before the *Word* was made *flesh* are described in the writings of the prophets.

It is well known that the most glorious appearance, through the *Shekinah* <note>original: *Schechinah* — the visible manifestation of God’s presence, often as a cloud or light</note>, occurred with all the majesty and honors due to the presence of the God of *Israel*, who gave the law to the *Hebrew* church and who received all its acts of religious worship. This appearance was received, respected, and honored as the presence of *Jehovah*. Since this has been understood for many reasons to be an appearance of the *Logos* <note>original Greek: λογος — the Word</note>, I believe it shows what was most intentionally meant by the phrase *being in the form of God, and being equal with God*: that is, to be revealed in the majesty and with the authority of the true God, and to receive the honors and worship equal to the majesty and authority of the true God. This was how the *Shekinah* appeared; this was how the *Shekinah* was honored and worshiped in its appearances as *Jehovah*, the God of *Israel*.

It is rightly observed that this appearance through the *Shekinah* is styled by the Greek interpreters <note>Referring to the translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament</note> as *the Glory* or *the Glory of God*.

# the LOGOS considered.

*...wonders, and signs, which God did through him in the midst of you, as you yourselves also know.* <note>Acts 2:22</note>

It seems clear then, that it is in no way necessary to apply what is spoken in general about the *Messiah* <note>original: "Christ"</note> specifically to the *Word made flesh* <note>the Logos, or divine nature</note>. This is because many things are spoken of him only as the *Son of Man*, many things are spoken of him as being *under the guidance of the Spirit*, and many things are spoken of him which cannot be understood as referring to the *Word*.

When we apply this observation to the scriptures being discussed, it becomes clear that they cannot apply to *Jesus* as the *Word*, or in his divine nature.

In these texts, *Christ* is called the *Son*: *The Son can do nothing of himself; whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise* <note>John 5:19</note>. *Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son.* <note>Mark 13:32</note> This expression, *the Son*, is frequently used concerning *Jesus* the *Messiah* in his role as the *Son of Man*. Because it is very rarely or never meant to refer to *the Word*, it leads us naturally to understand it as referring to his human nature. There is no necessity, and no specific reason within the texts themselves, to understand them as referring to *the Word*, or to *Christ* in his highest capacity. Therefore, nothing can be concluded from any expressions in them regarding an inferiority in the metaphysical essence <note>the fundamental nature or being</note> of *the Word*, whatever those expressions may be.

Furthermore, there does not seem to be any great difficulty in a point that some people think is very significant: that *the Son* is named after *the angels in heaven*, and must therefore be considered in his highest capacity. Since the Son of Man is the final prophet of the Church and is appointed to be the judge on the last day, he is the most logical person to receive such a message. If a specific time—which is unknown in itself and only made certain by the choice and determination of God's will—was to be made known to humanity through a revelation, was not this great revealer of God more likely to receive such a revelation from Him than any angel or archangel?

Since the Scriptures are the rule for our faith and judgment, I leave my interpretations of them—uninfluenced by the authority of any men—to the serious and impartial examination of my readers, as is only appropriate.

His lordship had too much sense to deny the certainty of all historical evidence regarding past facts (as some have been willing to do) or to insist upon eye-witness demonstration for events that took place in former ages. ## PART I.

### *On the Study and Use of HISTORY.*

The late Lord Bolingbroke <note>Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke (1678–1751), was a prominent English politician and philosopher known for his influential—and often controversial—writings on politics and religion.</note> has generally earned the reputation of being one of the finest writers in our language. This has granted him a kind of authority in the world, which clears the way for an easy and favorable reception of anything that is published under his name. A writer possessed of such talents has it in his power to be remarkably helpful <note>original: "signally serviceable"</note> to religion and the true interest of his country; and on the other hand, there is scarcely anything of more harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note> influence than such talents when they are misapplied. When the public was first informed of letters written by him on the study and use of history, it was natural to expect something very entertaining and improv-

And it will not be denied that he has many good and some very curious observations, expressed in a very polite <note>original: "genteel"</note> manner, and with great elegance and purity of style; but these are interspersed with others of a very different kind, and of a dangerous tendency.

In these letters, his lordship has done what he could to expose the authority of the Scriptures to contempt; at the same time, he has made the most unfavorable <note>original: "disadvantageous"</note> representation of the present state of the government and constitution of his country. If we are to trust the accounts he gives us, Christianity has no real foundation of factual truth to depend upon; it has been upheld by superstition, ignorance, and fraud <note>original: "imposture"</note>; and it has been visibly decaying ever since the revival of learning and knowledge. And our civil constitution, instead of being improved by the late Revolution <note>The Glorious Revolution of 1688, which overthrew King James II and established a constitutional monarchy under William III and Mary II.</note>, has been growing worse ever since; and our liberties are in more real danger than they were before. 

The natural tendency of such representations is to inspire a thorough contempt and disregard for the religion into which we were baptized, and to produce endless jealousies and discontents—if not open insurrections—against the government under which we live. No man, therefore, who has a just zeal for either of these, can see such an insolent attempt against both without concern. And, in this case, the rank <note>original: "quality"</note>, the ability, and the reputation of the writer, as it makes the attempt more dangerous, renders it more necessary to guard against

He frequently expresses himself in those reflections as one superior to fortune and exile, and as one who had attained a perfect philosophical calmness and tranquility, whose mind was not to be disturbed <note>original: “discomposed”</note> by any outward evils. And who would not be inclined to hold a high regard for the sentiments of a great genius? From his youth, he had always loved study and desired knowledge, and to this he added industry and application. He had an opportunity to retire from the world and knew how to make the most of it <note>original: “improve it”</note>; and he had used his solitude to contemplate himself, others, and all the things of this world through the lens <note>original: “medium”</note> of pure and undefiled reason!

But for now, I only mention it as proof of the desire he possessed to appear to think in a way different from, and superior to, the rest of mankind—even the learned world. Such a desire and craving for novelty, and for thinking outside the common path, can lead people of great talent <note>original: "parts"</note> astray in their search for truth, and it has often done so.

But there are other passions and feelings <note>original: "affections"</note> that have an even less friendly influence and are likely to give a wrong bias to the mind. He represents the Members of Parliament as viewing parliamentary business only as a trade. My only goal in making these observations is to prevent us from being too strongly biased in favor of a writer who is so distinguished by his talents and who presents such a deceptive <note>original: "specious"</note> appearance of authority.

I will now proceed to a more detailed <note>original: "distinct"</note> examination of Lord *Bolingbroke’s* Letters.

In them, we find—as has already been suggested—many good and excellent observations regarding the study and use of history. These are delivered with great clarity of expression and appropriate <note>original: "propriety"</note> sentiment. His instructions <note>original: "directions"</note> are full of good sense, and many of them are very effectively illustrated by suitable and well-chosen examples <note>original: "instances"</note>. In general, it must be admitted that his observations concerning the usefulness of history, the advantages he attributes <note>original: "afcribes"</note> to it, and the goals <note>original: "ends"</note> to be sought through it are mostly accurate <note>original: "just"</note>. ...this, along with the examples it provides <note>original: "affordeth"</note> (while he discards other methods as being of little or no use), was the best and only school of virtue, the most universal and necessary means of instruction, and alone sufficient to make us good men and good citizens, and to provide <note>original: "furnish"</note> us with all the knowledge <note>original: "knowlege"</note> that is appropriate <note>original: "proper"</note> for our guidance <note>original: "direction"</note> in practice. He observes—That “history is philosophy, teaching us by example how to conduct ourselves in all the positions <note>original: "stations"</note> of private and public life”—and that—“it is, above all others, the most appropriate <note>original: "proper"</note> way to train us in public and private virtue.*” He declares that—“everyone who is able to read, and to reflect upon what he reads, is able to make that use of history which he recommends; and everyone who does so will find, in his own way <note>original: "in his degree"</note>, the benefit that arises from an early acquaintance with mankind, gained <note>original: "contracted"</note> through this method.†” He adds that—“we are only passengers or travelers <note>original: "sojourners"</note> in this world, but we are absolute strangers during the first steps we take in it. Our guides are often ignorant or unfaithful. But by this map of the country which history spreads before us, we may learn, if we please, to guide ourselves.” So, history is the guide he proposes to all people to lead them on their journey through this world, and by which every person is capable of guiding themselves in all the situations and circumstances of public and private life.

<header>Reflections on the Late</header>

History is, no doubt, very useful in its proper place; but there are other means of instruction to be joined with it in order for it to achieve its purpose <note>original: "answering the end"</note>. It is not meant to serve in place of everything, nor to supersede all other methods of instruction. We need to be well-seasoned and grounded <note>original: "principled"</note> with a just sense of the moral differences between things, and with the excellent rules of religion and the important considerations it sets <note>original: "setteth"</note> before us. This allows us to form just opinions <note>original: "sentiments"</note> of things, to make a right use of history for our improvement in virtue, and to know how to properly apply the examples it provides <note>original: "furnisheth"</note>. 

Accordingly, our author himself insists that we must apply ourselves to history—"in a philosophical spirit and manner*." He observes that—"particular examples in history may be of use sometimes in particular cases, but that the application of them is dangerous." He would have a person, therefore, study history as one would study philosophy. And in the account he gives in his third letter of what is necessary in order to make a right use of history, he carries it so far—and really makes the work so difficult—as to be beyond what can be expected from the majority of mankind. He concludes by saying that—"by such methods as these, a man of parts <note>original: "a man of parts" refers to a person of great ability or talent</note> may improve the study of history to its proper and principal use†." In this, he seems <note>original: "seemeth"</note> to represent making a right use of history as a very difficult thing, which none but people of talent...

and then to proceed to the histories of particular countries, nations, and ages. And this appears to be a very reasonable and natural method. And if *Bodin* proposes taking a large scope and compass in reading history, his lordship <note>Lord Bolingbroke</note>, though he seems here to blame him for it, sometimes expresses himself in a manner that looks no less extensive. For he recommends the reading of history of all kinds—of civilized and uncivilized, of ancient and modern nations—as necessary to give us a right knowledge of the human species and of ourselves. He observes in his fifth letter that:

> “Man is the subject of every history; and to know him well, we must see him and consider him as history alone can present him to us: in every age, in every country, in every state, in life, and in death. History, therefore, of all kinds—of civilized and uncivilized, of ancient and modern nations—in short, all history that descends to a sufficient detail of human actions and characters, is useful to bring us acquainted with our species, nay, with ourselves*.”

And particularly with respect to ancient history, he mentions it in his second letter as a great advantage that:

> “In ancient history, the beginning, the progression, and the end appear—not of particular reigns, much less of particular enterprises or systems of policy alone—but of governments, of nations, of empires, and of all the various systems that have succeeded one another in the course of their duration‡.”

And yet he afterwards seems to confine our attention to modern history. He will allow us indeed to *read* the histories of former ages and nations, because it would be shameful to be entirely ignorant of them; but he would not have us *study* any histories except those of the last two centuries. That these deserve particular attention will easily be acknowledged for several reasons; and, among others, for that which he assigns: the great change that has been brought about in the civil and ecclesiastical <note>original: "eccleſiaſtical policy"; referring to the governance and affairs of the church.</note> policy of these parts of the world since the end of the fifteenth century, of which he gives an elegant representation in his sixth letter. 

But certainly there are many things in the histories of preceding ages—both in other countries and in our own—that well deserve to be not only read, but thoroughly considered by us. These are capable of providing very useful reflections and achieving those excellent goals for which he had recommended the study of history in the earlier part of these letters. This might easily be shown, if it were in any doubt, regarding both civil and ecclesiastical history.

But, not to dwell any longer on this and some other observations that might be made on particular passages in these letters, I shall proceed to the main purpose of these remarks: namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, to consider those things in them which might be misused, or which appear to have a harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note> tendency. My remarks shall be organized under three headings.

I shall first consider the reflections he has cast upon literature.

And then I shall proceed to those passages in his *Letters* which are designed to expose [critically] the Holy Scriptures and the Christian religion.

And, lastly, I shall take some notice of the several reflections he has made upon the consequences of the late Revolution <note>The Glorious Revolution of 1688, which overthrew King James II and established the constitutional monarchy.</note> and the state of affairs under the present Establishment.

It may seem a little surprising that such a refined <note>original: "polite"</note> writer—and one who, as he lets us know, has always loved study and application since his youth—should yet, in several parts of these *Letters*, express himself in a manner that seems calculated to show contempt for learning and to discourage men from applying themselves to the pursuit of it. Every friend of learning should, I think, acknowledge that respect is due to those who, in their various ways, have contributed to promote it. It is a pursuit that even Sir *Isaac Newton* judged to be worthy of his great genius. 

One would think that any fair-minded person who truly values learning would have great respect for those who have taken the pains to clarify these matters. And where absolute certainty cannot be reached, a well-informed guess <note>original: "happy conjecture"</note> can be both pleasing and useful.

It looks a little odd that there is no kind of men for whom, throughout these Letters, he shows less regard than for those who are generally accounted men of learning. Speaking of those who—"affect the reputation of great scholars, at the expense of groping all their lives in the dark mazes of antiquity"—he says that—"all these mistake the true design of study, and the true use of history." 

Great as the advantages are that he ascribes to history—and which he thinks every man is capable of who is able to read and to reflect upon what he reads—yet, "a creditable kind of ignorance is, in his opinion, the whole benefit which the generality even of the most learned reap from it." And he intimates that the only effect of their reading and studying history is to become pedants; that is <note>original: i.e.; abbreviation for id est</note>, as he explains it—"worse than ignorant, always incapable, sometimes meddling and presuming *."

In his third Letter on the study of history, he sets himself to consider the state of ancient history, both sacred and secular <note>original: "profane"; in this context, "profane history" simply means non-religious or secular history</note>: and begins by declaring his resolution——

His accounts are short because he stayed close to the truth and took care to record no more of those times than he had good information on, or than was necessary for the goal he had in view. This goal seems principally to have been to give a brief account of the creation, the formation of the first human pair, their placement in Paradise, the fall, and the flood—which were the most remarkable events of that period—and to continue the lineage from Adam through Seth to Noah, as he later does from Noah to Abraham.

And just as the *Hebrew* language was not absolutely forgotten among the *Jews* during their captivity, neither were their Sacred Books entirely lost. Indeed, it would be absurd to suppose so. That captivity lasted seventy years from its first beginning under *Jehoiakim* <note>King of Judah whose reign saw the first Babylonian sieges</note>; however, from the time of the total destruction of *Jerusalem* and the Temple, and the deportation of the final remnant of the people to *Babylon*, it lasted only about fifty years. There were many among those who had been deported from *Jerusalem* who survived the entire period and lived to return. *“Many of the priests and Levites, and the heads of the families—who were elderly men <note>original: "antient men"</note> and had seen the first Temple—wept with a loud voice when the foundation of this second Temple was laid before their eyes”* (Ezra 3:12). 

All those among them who lived to be seventy or eighty years old were twenty or thirty years old when *Jerusalem* and the *Temple* were destroyed. To suggest that these people would entirely forget their language, or their religion, history, and laws, is highly improbable <note>original: "very absurd"</note>. Furthermore, the people expected a deliverance and restoration to their own land, as the prophets had assured them. This hope would naturally make them more diligent in preserving their laws and the ancient, authentic records and memorials of their nation. It appears from the account of those who returned that many of the *Priests*, the *Levites*, the *Singers*, and the *Gatekeepers* <note>original: "Porters"</note>...

The most remarkable part of Jewish history is that which is contained in the books of **Moses**. It is there that we find an account of the first constitution of their <term>sacred polity</term> <note>The "sacred polity" refers to the theocratic system of government and religious law established for the Israelites</note>. All that follows from the text is that upon that occasion, and at that time, *Noah* pronounced a remarkable prediction conveying favors and blessings upon *Shem* and *Japheth* and their descendants, and that the descendants of *Canaan* (one of *Ham*’s sons) should be in a low and servile condition, subjected to both those of *Shem* and *Japheth*. 

It was not in a passion or a drunken fit that *Noah* pronounced this, as his lordship <note>Lord Bolingbroke</note> seems willing to represent it; but God was pleased on that occasion to enlighten *Noah* with a vision of the fates of his descendants. That part of the prediction that relates to *Shem* and *Japheth* seems to be of a noble extent and looks a great way forward, as many have observed, which I shall not inquire into now. And as to that part of the prophecy which relates to *Canaan*, it is recorded by *Moses* that when it came to be

The Christian theologians <note>original: "divines"</note> are willing to engage with this point <note>original: "join issue on this point"</note>. The best and most appropriate way of proving the truth of ancient facts is undoubtedly through authentic accounts published in the age in which the facts occurred and transmitted to our own times with sufficient marks of credibility. Several things are to be considered in order for us to judge whether, and to what extent, those accounts may be depended upon:

*   If the facts related there were of a public nature, performed for the most part in ***open view***, and for which an appeal is made to numerous witnesses.
*   If the accounts of those facts were given by persons who were perfectly well-acquainted with the events and who, having had full opportunity to know them, were themselves absolutely persuaded of the truth and reality of those facts.
*   If they appear from their whole character to have been persons of great integrity <note>original: "probity"</note> and guileless sincerity <note>original: "undesigning simplicity"</note>, who could have no worldly interest to serve by faking or disguising those facts.
*   If their prejudices did not have any tendency to bias them in favor of those facts, but rather the contrary.
*   If the writings themselves have all the characteristics of genuine simplicity and an impartial regard for truth that can be reasonably desired.
*   If they can be clearly traced from the age in which they were written and the facts were said to be done, through the succeeding ages, to our own times.

Several factors must be considered in order for us to judge whether, and to what extent, those accounts may be relied upon:

*   First, if the facts related there were of a public nature, performed for the most part in open view, and supported by an appeal to a great number of witnesses.
*   Second, if the accounts of those facts were provided by people who were perfectly well-acquainted with them and who, having had full opportunity to know them, were themselves absolutely convinced of the truth and reality of those facts.
*   Third, if they appear by their whole character to have been persons of great integrity <note>original: "probity"</note> and honest simplicity <note>original: "undesigning simplicity"</note>, who could have no worldly interest to serve by faking or disguising those facts.
*   Fourth, if their personal prejudices did not have any tendency to bias them in favor of those facts, but rather the opposite.
*   Fifth, if the writings themselves have all the characteristics of genuine simplicity and an impartial regard for the truth that can be reasonably desired.
*   Sixth, if they can be clearly traced from the age in which they were written—and the time the facts were said to have occurred—through the succeeding ages to our own times.

# Reflections on the Late

The actions and teachings <note>original: "discourses"</note> of our Lord were well known among the Christians of the first century <note>original: "age"</note>, both through written accounts and through traditions received from the preaching of the Apostles. This certainly confirms, rather than weakens, the accounts given in the *Gospels*; it assumes that the facts recorded there were already well-known and considered authoritative. 

However, the author should not claim it as a fact accepted by all scholars that those first-century Church Fathers used other Gospels besides those written by the Evangelists <note>The "Evangelists" traditionally refers to the four authors of the canonical Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note>. The only passage among all the works of the Apostolic Fathers <note>The "Apostolic Fathers" were early Christian writers believed to have had personal contact with the Apostles.</note> that seems to suggest this is one by *Ignatius*. Some believe this passage was taken from the *Gospel of the Hebrews*—which itself was actually *St. Matthew's Gospel* with some later additions and changes. Yet, that passage can be fairly interpreted as referring to the words of our Savior recorded by *St. Luke*, Chapter 24, verse 39 *.

Indeed, we can gather from the introduction to *St. Luke's Gospel* that many people in that first century had attempted to write a history of our Savior's life, miracles, and teachings. Thus we find, by the acknowledgment of friends and enemies who lived closest to those times, that the accounts contained in the books of the Evangelists <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> were written in the apostolic age—the age in which the facts recorded there are said to have happened. There are clear references to them, and passages quoted from them, in the few writings that remain from the first century. 

In the age immediately following, we have full proof that they were universally accepted in the Christian church as having divine authority. They were read as such in Christian assemblies and were attributed by name to Christ’s own immediate followers or their close companions: *Matthew*, *Mark*, *Luke*, and *John*. This has been universally admitted in all ages since then, and these books have been passed down to our times with such continuous and uninterrupted evidence as cannot be produced for any other books whatsoever. 

A person would be considered very unreasonable if they denied, or even questioned, whether the books of *Livy*, *Sallust*, or *Tacitus* <note>Titus Livius, Sallust, and Tacitus were famous Roman historians whose works are fundamental to our understanding of ancient history.</note> were written by the men whose names they bear. It suggests that there are no certain principles at all, even in natural religion or morality; since every principle—even those relating to the existence and perfections of God, divine Providence, a future state, and the natural distinctions between good and evil—has been disputed <note>original: "controverted"</note>, even by people who claimed <note>original: "pretended"</note> to be learned, wise, and philosophical. 

But the absurdity of this way of arguing is very evident. The principle that anything that has been disputed is therefore uncertain is fallacious. One might as well say that whatever is capable of being abused is neither good nor useful. It does not follow that the Scriptures are not sufficiently clear and definite <note>original: "determinate"</note> to serve as a rule of faith and practice in everything essential or necessary for salvation, simply because there have been men in every age who have interpreted them in different ways. It would also require Him to exert His divine power in an extraordinary manner to subdue or remove all their prejudices, overrule their different passions, temperaments <note>original: "humours"</note>, inclinations, and interests, and place them all in exactly the same situation and circumstances.

It is no argument against the certainty or clarity <note>original: "perspicuity"</note> of the sacred text. Laws may be of great use, even if they do not absolutely prevent trickery <note>original: "chicanery"</note> and evasion. It is never a sound argument to claim that the Scriptures are not a reliable guide simply because people disagree. Such an argument would also prove that no revelation God could possibly provide could ever serve as a standard for faith and practice, or be of any use in guiding people toward truth and happiness. 

If God were to reveal His will to instruct humanity in what is most important for them to know and to direct them toward salvation—a possibility that no Theist <note>term: a person who believes in the existence of a god or gods, specifically a creator who intervenes in the universe</note> can deny—and if He were to establish a set of laws and doctrines for this purpose, it is questionable whether it could ever be made so clear and explicit that everyone throughout all ages would agree on its meaning. 

This could hardly be expected unless God were to miraculously intervene <note>original: "interpose"</note> with an irresistible influence to force everyone to think the same way. He would have to give everyone the exact same ideas, the same levels of natural talent, and identical opportunities for education <note>original: "acquired improvement"</note>. He would have to grant them all the same wisdom <note>original: "sagacity"</note>, the same leisure, and the same diligence. He would also need to use His divine power in an extraordinary way to suppress or remove all their prejudices, and to override their various passions, temperaments <note>original: "humours"</note>, inclinations, and interests, placing everyone in exactly the same situation and

And this would be by no means consistent with the wisdom of the divine government, or with the nature of man and his freedom as a moral agent <note>term: a being capable of acting with reference to right and wrong</note>, and with the methods and orders of Providence <note>term: God's protective care and guidance over the world</note>. Nor is there any necessity for such an extraordinary intervention <note>original: "procedure"</note>. For it would be absurd to the highest degree to claim that the Scripture can be of no use to anyone unless everyone agreed about it; or to claim that it is not sufficiently clear to fulfill its purpose <note>original: "answer the end"</note> just because there are some people who pervert or abuse it.

Yet, after all the noise <note>original: "clamour"</note> that has been raised about the differences among Christians regarding the meaning <note>original: "sense"</note> of Scripture, there are many things of great importance about which there has been, in all ages, a very general agreement among professed Christians. 

They agree that there is one God, who made heaven and earth and all things within them; that he preserves all things by the word of his power and governs all things by his Providence; that he is infinitely powerful, wise, and good, and is to be loved, feared, adored, and obeyed above all else. They also agree that just as there is one God, there is also one Mediator <note>term: a person who acts as a link between two parties; in Christian theology, Jesus Christ is the link between God and humanity</note> between God and man: ***Jesus Christ*** the ***righteous***, whom he, in his infinite love and mercy, sent into the world to save and to redeem us. They agree that he came to instruct us by his doctrine, to bring a clear revelation of the divine will, and to set before us a bright and most perfect example for us to imitate. Finally, they agree that he submitted to the most painful <note>original: "grievous"</note> sufferings, and to death itself, for our sakes, so that he

# Lord Bolingbroke’s Letters.

Although there are many contentions <note>original: "contentions," meaning disputes or arguments</note> about things of little or no importance <note>original: "moment"</note>, this is no argument against the divine authority or usefulness of the sacred writings. Those who distort <note>original: "wrest"</note> the *Scriptures* must be accountable to him who gave them for that perversion and abuse, just as men must be accountable for the abuse of their reason. But this is far from proving that the Scriptures therefore serve no valuable purpose and could not be of a divine origin. 

Still, it is true that whoever will apply himself to read and consider the Holy Scriptures—with a teachable and attentive mind, an upright intention to know and do the will of God, and a humble dependence on God’s gracious assistance—will find vast advantages. These writings will instruct him in the knowledge of religion, engage him in its practice, and guide him in the way of salvation.

It appears, then, that the foundation on which his "formidable dilemma" <note>This refers to a logical trap or difficult choice posed by Lord Bolingbroke in his writings.</note> is built will not hold. There is, at this time, a *standard for Christianity*: specifically, the doctrines and laws of our Savior and his Apostles as contained in the Holy Scriptures. It must be, and is, acknowledged by all who profess themselves Christians that whatever is revealed in those sacred books is true and certain, and whatever can be shown to be contrary to what is revealed there is false. 

The *Roman Catholics* <note>original: "Romanists"</note> as well as *Protestants* own the divinity and authenticity of the sacred text. Although for their own particular views the Catholics would join unwritten traditions with it and are in favor of giving the church alone the authority to interpret...

However, without diving too deeply into the matter, one might venture to say—without being considered lost to all sense of shame—that no matter how good the intentions of the managers <note>original: "managers"; refers to the Tory ministers, including Bolingbroke, who directed the peace negotiations</note> might have been, some of the measures they took were very poorly chosen, either for preserving the union among the allies or for obtaining an advantageous peace from *France*.

These being the measures that were taken in *England*, can it be imagined that so shrewd <note>original: "politic"</note> a court as that of *France* would not seize such an advantage and exploit it? The French were, undoubtedly, very desirous of peace; but they also knew that the *British* ministry must and would have a peace. Therefore, they knew that by holding out a little longer, they would obtain peace upon much more advantageous terms for *France* than they previously had reason to expect. 

And so eager was the *British* ministry to get rid of the war that, although they had given the *Dutch* positive assurances at the beginning of the year 1712 that they would act vigorously in the common cause, only two months later—at the start of the military campaign—orders were sent in the Queen’s name to the *British* general <note>The Duke of Ormond, who replaced the Duke of Marlborough as commander-in-chief</note> not to engage in any siege or battle until further orders. This was done in coordination <note>original: "concert"</note> with the *French*, the common enemy, and without the knowledge or involvement of the allies. This action was soon followed by a ceasefire <note>original: "cessation of arms"</note>, by an actual separation of the national *British* troops from the alliance, and by an effort to pull all the foreign troops in *British* pay away from the rest of the confederate army. This was a strange and extraordinary measure, if considered in all its circumstances.

circumstances. And his lordship’s <note>Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke</note> justification of it is almost as extraordinary. I shall not examine it, though if I were inclined to do so, I would not ask for a better advantage than he has provided. Those who are not familiar with his lordship’s style will likely wonder at the peculiar tone of confidence with which he expresses himself on this occasion.

After having accused the Dutch Republic <note>original: "the states," referring to the States-General of the Netherlands</note> of arrogance and presumption for finding fault with the Queen’s <note>Queen Anne</note> measures, he insists that if they had made proper use of the two-month suspension <note>The cessation of hostilities in 1712</note> by joining with the Queen—“even then we might have resumed the superiority we began to lose in the congress <note>The peace negotiations at Utrecht</note>*.” ———

This is an honest admission that from the time those orders <note>The "restraining orders" given to the Duke of Ormond not to fight the French</note> were given to the *British* general, we began to lose that superiority in the peace conference which he had previously acknowledged we held at the beginning of the year 1712 †. And indeed, I cannot see how it could be otherwise; since, by this step, the *French* clearly saw that *England* was determined not to carry on the war any longer. Nor, after such a step, would it have been in the power of the Queen and the *Dutch* together to regain that superiority in the negotiations which they had lost—unless *France* had been persuaded that, if they did not agree to the terms the allies thought necessary, *Great Britain* would join heartily in pursuing the war.

But I shall not dwell any longer on these matters, as it is not my intention to conduct a detailed examination of what he has offered in defense <note>original: "vindication"</note> of the Peace of Utrecht. I shall only add this one further remark regarding it: throughout his writing, he maintains the favorite style of that era, speaking of "the Queen’s peace" and "the Queen’s measures." Any opposition against the ministry of that time, and the measures they were taking, is constantly represented as a kind of high treason against her Majesty and an insult to her royal authority. However, since that time, his lordship has learned very well how to distinguish between the King and his ministers; he has since treated it as great insolence for a ministry to hide <note>original: "screen"</note> their measures under the shadow of royal authority.

After having so vehemently spoken out against the *Whigs* <note>The political faction that supported the war against France and the Hanoverian succession</note> for being so eager to carry on the war during *Queen Anne’s* reign, his lordship finds just as much fault with them for the overly peaceful disposition they showed afterward. He observes that—

> "A rage for war possessed a party in our nation until the death of the late Queen; a rage for negotiating has possessed the same party of men ever since †."

# Reflections on the Late
->Lord Bolingbroke's Letters<-

...ministers were in the right or wrong while managing their negotiations. I leave this to those who understand these matters better than I can pretend to do, and about which men of excellent sense and understanding may probably differ in their opinions <note>original: "sentiments"</note>. 

I shall only observe how impossible it is for that party of men <note>The Whigs</note> to please his lordship. He has declared such a fixed hatred <note>original: "aversion"</note> toward them, and he claims they have held the administration <note>The government</note> in their hands almost ever since the Revolution <note>The Glorious Revolution of 1688, which overthrew James II</note>. Whether they go to war or negotiate, they are always in the wrong. His lordship has mentioned what he calls a "twofold rage": a rage for warring and a rage for negotiating. 

There is a third rage just as remarkable as either of those: the rage of a party spirit. This spirit leads men to put the worst spin on things and give everything the most offensive <note>original: "odious"</note> interpretation. Hardly any measures can be taken in political matters that are not subject to objections and inconveniences. When these measures fall into the hands of someone with such brilliant talent <note>original: "bright parts"</note> and such a great command of words as the late Lord **Bolingbroke**, they can be made to appear in a very unfavorable light. 

And yet, perhaps the people he blames were not as wrong, or as inconsistent with themselves as he represents them, for supporting war first and then negotiation later. He himself admits that the war entered into against **France** was necessary for several years and that it was carried out with surprising success. The **Whigs** were in favor of continuing...

...to continue the war—even though the nation was heavily burdened—until they had effectively broken and humbled *French* power and had reaped advantages equal to such unparalleled successes. They could consistently hold this opinion, and yet later—once the opportunity had slipped away and could not be recovered, the peace was signed, and the alliance <note>original: "confederacy"</note> dissolved—they might oppose plunging the nation into new wars. Such new conflicts would only increase the debt that had been necessarily incurred before. 

And if, to prevent such new wars, they sometimes pushed their desire for negotiation too far—appearing peaceful even to the point of submissiveness <note>original: "tameness"</note>—others might find fault with them. However, his lordship <note>Lord Bolingbroke</note> and those who share his views had no right to complain. After all, they had so bitterly attacked the Whigs for being eager to continue a war in which they had such glorious prospects. 

For certainly, if the nation being exhausted and overburdened with debt was a reason to end that glorious and successful war with a peace treaty—a peace that failed to meet its goals or reap the advantages that might have been expected—then this reason was even stronger for avoiding new wars. In new conflicts, they could not guarantee the same success, and the consequences would be difficult to predict. Therefore, even if their treaties and negotiations were not handled as successfully in every respect as his lordship, in his superior wisdom, might think they should have been,

yet he should at least have commended their peaceful <note>original: "pacific"</note> intention. It is proper to observe that since he wrote his long letter on the Peace of *Utrecht*, there has been another war that could not be avoided. This was in addition to a dangerous rebellion at home <note>likely referring to the Jacobite rising of 1745, which sought to restore the Stuart monarchy</note>, which has caused new and vast expenses and has greatly increased the national debt, which was already so large. 

But the administration is not to be blamed; they stayed out of that war as long as they could, until the voice of the nation demanded it. Much less are they to be blamed for that rebellion, which was started with the goal of overturning the current government <note>original: "present establishment"</note>. And yet the enemies of our constitution are so unreasonable as to cry out against the government for the expenses and debts made necessary by a war that the whole nation demanded and a rebellion that they themselves had started.

I have now finished my remarks on the late Lord *Bolingbroke’s* *Letters on the Study and Use of History*. I regret that I have found it necessary to say many things that may seem to reflect poorly on the reputation of such an eminent writer. However, I believe that by now it is clear that, however great his abilities may be, his confident assertions cannot be fully relied upon—not even in civil and political matters, and much less in religious ones. It is deeply concerning to see such blatant attempts made against what should be dearer to us than our lives <note>the author refers here to the Christian religion and the British system of government, both of which he feels Bolingbroke undermined</note>.
